First, give it a preference worth saving: print(chat( "Remember that I prefer Python and use uv " "for managing my projects." )) Output: I'll remember that you prefer Python and use `uv` to manage your projects. Next, ask a related question: print(chat( "How should I set up my next Python project?" )) Output: I remember you prefer Python and use **uv** for project management. A solid setup: ```bash uv init my-project cd my-project uv add <runtime-dependency> uv add --dev pytest ruff mypy ``` The agent can retrieve the saved preference with search_memory() and use it to make the response more relevant. Because the memory is stored in Mem0, it can still be retrieved even after the Python application is restarted. Giving OpenCode the Same Memory We can also give a coding agent such as OpenCode persistent memory without writing the Python tools ourselves. Mem0 provides an official hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with tools for adding, searching, updating, and deleting memories. Add it to OpenCode with: npx mcp-add \ --name mem0-mcp \ --type http \ --url "https://mcp.mem0.ai/mcp" \ --clients "opencode" Restart OpenCode and test it: Remember that I prefer uv instead of pip for new Python projects. Then start a new session and ask: How should I initialize this Python project? OpenCode can retrieve the stored preference through the Mem0 MCP tools. Mem0 currently exposes operations including add_memory , search_memories , get_memories , update_memory , delete_memory , and more. You can verify the connection with: opencode mcp list Final Thoughts ChatGPT has a memory feature that can remember useful information from previous conversations and bring it back in later sessions. That is why it can sometimes feel like ChatGPT already understands what you are trying to say without you having to explain everything again. You can create a similar experience in your own AI applications. For example, you can build an assistant that remembers customer preferences, an internal tool that keeps track of important decisions, or a coding agent that remembers your preferred frameworks, project rules, and development habits. The main benefit is that users do not have to start from scratch every time. The agent can retrieve relevant information from earlier sessions and use it to give more personalized and consistent responses. In this guide, we learned how AI agent memory works, how short-term and long-term memory differ, and how to use Mem0 with the OpenAI Agents SDK to save and retrieve memories. We also connected the same memory system to OpenCode through MCP. Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies.

title: Top 7 Python Libraries for Time Series Analysis and Modeling
abstract: Top 7 Python Libraries for Time Series Analysis and Modeling Working with time series data? These Python libraries cover everything from classical forecasting to deep learning and anomaly detection. By Bala Priya C , KDnuggets Contributing Editor & Technical Content Specialist on November 6, 2026 in Python Introduction Time series analysis has one of the most fragmented library ecosystems in Python. Depending on whether you need statistical forecasting, machine learning pipelines, deep learning models, or anomaly detection, you'll reach for different tools — each with its own API, data format expectations, and assumptions about your problem. This article covers seven useful Python libraries that collectively span the full spectrum of time series work, including: Classical and automated statistical forecasting Scalable machine learning pipelines and model selection Deep learning and ensemble-based forecasting Anomaly detection, outlier analysis, and motif discovery Let's explore them. 1. Building Statistical Forecasting Models with statsmodels When interpretability is just as important as predictive power, statsmodels is the first library to reach for. It is the foundation of classical time series analysis in Python, implementing the statistical models that have been workhorses in economics, finance, and operations research for decades. What makes statsmodels useful: Implements the full ARIMA family, including ARIMA and SARIMAX for seasonal data and exogenous regressors, with confidence intervals, Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criterion (BIC) scores, and diagnostic plots included in the output Provides exponential smoothing models through ETSModel , covering additive and multiplicative trend and seasonal components Includes statistical tests for pre-modeling diagnostics: the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test and KPSS test for stationarity, and the Ljung-Box test for residual autocorrelation Resources : statsmodels Time Series Analysis documentation and statsmodels examples 2. Automating Model Selection with pmdarima Finding the right ARIMA order — the (p, d, q) parameters — is one of the most tedious steps in classical forecasting. pmdarima solves this by bringing R's auto.arima functionality to Python, wrapping statsmodels under the hood and automating the model selection process. The following are the key features of pmdarima: auto_arima runs a stepwise search over candidate ARIMA orders, scoring by AIC or BIC, without manual interpretation of autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plots Follows scikit-learn 's fit/predict interface, so it slots into existing scikit-learn pipelines Tests for seasonality automatically before adding SARIMA terms, reducing the risk of forcing seasonal structure that isn't there Note : pmdarima is the right tool for a fast statistical baseline, or for automated forecasting across many series. Its GitHub repository shows development has slowed in recent releases, so check the changelog before pinning it into a new production pipeline. Resources : pmdarima documentation and pmdarima user guide 3. Building Unified Machine Learning Pipelines with sktime sktime provides a unified interface for time series learning tasks — forecasting, classification, regression, clustering, and annotation — spanning classical statistics, machine learning, and deep learning. It therefore tackles the fragmentation problem in Python's time series ecosystem that we started this article with. Why sktime should find a place in your time series toolkit: One consistent interface across estimators, so switching between an ARIMA model, a gradient boosting regressor, and a neural network is a small code change Composite model building — pipelining, ensembling, tuning, reduction — for chaining preprocessing and forecasting into a single reproducible workflow Time-series-aware cross-validation that respects temporal order, avoiding the leakage generic cross-validators introduce on sequential data Direct interfaces to related libraries, including scikit-learn, statsmodels, tsfresh , and PyOD sktime is the library to use when a workflow needs to be systematic, reproducible, and easy to compare across model families. Read Building Time-Series Machine Learning Models with sktime in Python for a practical introduction to sktime. Resources : sktime documentation and sktime Notebook Examples 4. Forecasting at Scale with Darts Darts takes a broader-toolkit approach than sktime. Instead of unifying access to other libraries' algorithms, it implements classical, machine learning, and deep learning models directly, with an emphasis on probabilistic forecasting and multi-series scale. What makes Darts interesting: Produces probabilistic forecasts across most models, returning prediction intervals rather than single-point estimates Trains a single global model across large collections of related series at once, rather than one model per series Includes a backtesting workflow for simulating historical forecasts across multiple horizons Ships an anomaly detection module that wraps forecasting or filtering models into detectors, or applies PyOD-style scorers directly to time series Darts also covers a broad model catalog in one package, spanning exponential smoothing, ARIMA, gradient-boosted regression, and several deep learning architectures. Resources : Darts documentation and Darts examples and tutorials 5. Detecting Temporal Patterns with stumpy Most time series libraries focus on forecasting. stumpy , however, computes the matrix profile, a structure recording the distance between every subsequence in a series and its nearest neighbor. That structure supports motif discovery, discord detection, and pattern discovery without labeled data. What makes stumpy helpful for pattern discovery in time series: Motif discovery surfaces the most frequently recurring subsequences — useful for sensor data, user activity logs, or equipment cycles, without labeling Discord detection finds the subsequences most unlike everything else, a parameter-light way to flag unusual events Scales through CPU parallelization and GPU acceleration for high-frequency or long-running data Supports additional tasks on top of the matrix profile, including shapelet discovery, streaming updates, and time series chains stumpy is often the right tool when the question is "what patterns exist in this data" rather than "what happens next." It complements forecasting libraries in production monitoring. Resources : stumpy documentation and stumpy GitHub repository 6. Scaling Anomaly Detection with PyOD For anomaly detection on tabular and multivariate feature matrices, PyOD is the most comprehensive library available. Its current major version implements more than 60 detection algorithms under one interface and has expanded beyond tabular data to also cover time series, graph, text, and image data. What makes PyOD useful for outlier detection: Covers the full spectrum in one package, including proximity-based, linear, ensemble, and deep learning methods One consistent interface across detectors, with continuous anomaly scores rather than only binary labels Utilities for parallel training and evaluation, cutting the boilerplate involved in building anomaly detection experiments Recent releases add agentic workflows for describing a detection task in plain language, on top of the existing programmatic API PyOD is still most often used on engineered feature matrices — rolling statistics, lag features, frequency components — rather than on raw sequences directly. Resources : PyOD documentation and PyOD GitHub repository 7. Forecasting with Deep Learning Using NeuralForecast When classical and machine learning-based models plateau, deep learning can close the gap. NeuralForecast by Nixtla brings a large collection of neural forecasting architectures to Python in a production-friendly package.

title: The components of agent memory
abstract: Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents. As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge. Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge. Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1). We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization. Claude can use dreaming to organize memory. This can correct mistakes, create notes, build new memory representations, or shape what’s preemptively loaded into future sessions. Memory notes By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window). In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory. Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next? Claude can write notes to memory. Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions. Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0 , a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions. Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future. We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using Claude Managed Agents . Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next. Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses. CL-Bench database task, comparing memory with a stateless baseline across models. Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong. Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3). Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher. Claude has learned to judge salience We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red , a game that challenges Claude to navigate complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4). We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game). Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md , and earned four badges. Claude’s memory directories for Sonnet 3.7 versus Fable 5 while playing Pokémon. Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself. Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down. Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works.

title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
abstract: 01 A three-step program AI for Science grantees Jakob Macke , Daniel Gedon , and Stefan Wahl are researchers at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the University of Tübingen, where they build AI tools for developing scientific models in neuroscience and beyond. In this guest post, they discuss how AI is starting to change scientific modeling. In 1951, Cambridge University’s computer went out of action for six months. This was inconvenient for physiologist Andrew Huxley, who, alongside his colleague Alan Hodgkin, had just built a set of equations to describe how a particular squid nerve cell fired. The scientists wanted to understand the “action potential” of these nerve cells: the electrical pulses they use to communicate, which underlie everything brains do, from perception to intelligence. The only way to find out whether the equations worked was to solve them and compare the solutions to data. Huxley had hoped to use the newfangled computer to solve the equations. Instead, he was forced to solve them using a hand-cranked mechanical calculator. It took him over three weeks. The basic structure of their model was dictated by known facts about the cell. Hodgkin and Huxley modeled its membrane as an electrical circuit. One part of the model, however, was just an educated guess. In order to make the curve fit the data they had measured, they found that they had to raise one variable to the fourth power—that is, to multiply it by itself three times. At the time, they did not know why. They just knew that otherwise the model didn’t predict the observed data as well. They did offer a hypothesis, however. They cautiously suggested that the variable in question, which governed how particular gates in the cell membrane opened, might require the fourth power because multiple charged particles in the membrane had to move into place before the gate would open. Decades later, long after both Hodgkin and Huxley had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1963, another team found the structure of a related potassium channel protein . And they discovered that, yes, it had four identical pieces arranged around a central pore . The model was fit to the data in 1951. Even then, it predicted how fast the impulse travels relatively accurately. More than that, it turned out to have helped predict the structure of potassium ion channels themselves, which it had never been fit to. Today, an AI system could plausibly find an equation like Hodgkin and Huxley’s in an afternoon, and perhaps it would fit the experimental data even more closely. But the point of the story is that simply knowing the fourth power did the job was not enough; what mattered was knowing that a simpler version of the model did not work. An AI system that merely hands you the model might give you an answer, but it does not give you understanding. Reproducing the data with a model is insufficient, because any number of models could do the same. What matters is being able to make claims about the real-world system itself, and ideally about other, similar systems. To do so, you need to know which features the model shares with other models that work, and which set it apart from models that don’t. As the mathematician Richard Hamming wrote in 1962, “The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.” A three-step program More than 70 years on, the Hodgkin-Huxley model remains the standard description of electrical activity in neurons. The same kinds of equations, with different constants, describe nerve cells across the animal kingdom, from squids to humans, even though our evolutionary lineages separated more than half a billion years ago. Even more important than its longevity, however, is what the Hodgkin-Huxley model tells us about how models work. Hodgkin and Huxley’s approach can be broken down into three steps, and most scientific modeling involves some version of them. The first is building the model. This means deciding what the model is made of and what shape its equations take. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s case, that meant the parts of the electrical circuit—the membrane and the gates—and the form of the equations, such as raising the underlying variable to the fourth power. The second is constraining the model—tuning its adjustable parameters to fit real measurements. For Hodgkin and Huxley, that included settings like how often the gates open under different voltages. The third is interpreting the model—asking what the model says about the real system, such as suggesting that the fourth power meant the gate had four moving parts. In practice, scientists go through these steps repeatedly . If the numbers fail to fit the measurements, or if the interpretation makes no sense, they go back and revise. All three steps were once done by people, but AI systems are increasingly involved in each of them. Machines have arguably made the most progress in constraining models, so we’ll start there. Splitting the bill, or how to constrain models When Hodgkin and Huxley constrained their model by eye and intuition, they ended up with a single set of numbers. This told them that the model could match the data. It didn’t tell them whether other numbers would have worked just as well or even better. Imagine you know that a group dinner added up to $120, but not who ordered what. Many different combinations of orders could have added up to that amount—perhaps everyone ordered a mid-priced burger, or perhaps one person had steak and lobster while everyone else had soup. Models of nerve cells work on the same principle: different combinations of gate parameters can produce near-identical electrical activity. Simply showing one combination that fits well hides all the other plausible parameter settings, and other combinations might have led to different predictions. This is true of almost any phenomenon being modeled. Many different sets of parameters can explain the observed data equally well. An illustration of constraining the Hodgkin-Huxley model. (1) A measurement from a nerve cell. (2) How likely the measurement is for each combination of potassium and sodium channel settings. Darker means a better fit. The blue dot is interactive. (3) Simulations of the model at three settings, compared to the measurement (gray). Some fit well, while others do not. The solution is a statistical method called Bayesian inference. It gives you every set of numbers that works reasonably well, as a probability distribution that takes into account their fit to the data and your prior knowledge about the parameters. The distribution takes the shape of a curve, with the best fits at the peak and the weaker ones at the fringes. But this method has usually been impractical for complex models, because it involves calculating how likely your measurements would be under every possible set of numbers. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s model, that would still be feasible, but for anything more complicated, it would be computationally impossible. For example, if each of the thousands of ion channels opens and closes at random, you would have to work out every combination. Returning to our restaurant bill analogy: it would be easy to answer, “If person A had the burger and person B had the steak, what would the bill come to?” but much harder to show which combinations could have led to the final bill, especially as the number of people and menu options grows. A different approach called simulation-based inference (SBI) overcomes this reverse-engineering problem with sheer computation. You pick random parameters, run the model, and record the output. You do it again and again— perhaps 100,000 times for a model like Hodgkin-Huxley , and millions of times for larger, more complex ones. Then you train a neural network on the results so that, given an output, it can return the range of parameters that could have produced it. All SBI requires is that you can run the model: put in a set of parameters and get back the kind of data you would expect to see.

title: Accelerating Reinforcement Learning Weight Refit with the Reshard Collective
abstract: During reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, training trajectories are generated on the fly by running inference with the current policy model. For training efficiency, it is common to run inference and training in parallel on separate GPU resources in a disaggregated setup. Although the policy model is updated only on the training GPUs, the system must periodically refresh the weights on the inference GPUs with the latest parameters generated on the training GPUs. This transfer of model weights between training and inference GPUs is called refit . Refit involves two defining characteristics that pose challenges. First, inference and training have different computational requirements, so the weights are distributed differently across inference and training instances by having different parallel mappings (data, context, tensor, expert, and pipeline parallelism). Second, because refit must update all model weights on the inference GPUs, the communication payload is on the order of the total size of the model’s weights. This payload is already very large for the latest frontier models and is expected to continue growing. Together, these characteristics mean that refit requires high-performance communication across a wide variety of distributed source and destination layouts. This post explains how AI training frameworks can address these refit challenges using the Reshard collective, a new type of collective communication primarily designed to accelerate RL weight refit. NCCL M2N Reshard, an open source reference implementation of the Reshard collective, is available through the NVIDIA/nccl-extensions GitHub repo. Challenges of current weight refit methods as models scale Existing refit implementations commonly use a gather-and-broadcast approach to handle differences between training and inference layouts. The typical gather-and-broadcast weight refit sequence for every model parameter is structured as follows: Training GPUs all-gather their local shards to reconstruct the complete parameter. The complete parameter tensor is broadcast to the inference GPUs. Each inference GPU retains the shard required by its local layout. Using the complete tensor as an intermediate representation makes it straightforward to transfer weights between different layouts. However, an inference GPU receives the full parameter even when it needs only a shard. This process creates redundant communication in both the gathering and broadcasting phases, which is suboptimal. The size of this communication grows with the model size, which continues to scale. For example, Kimi K3 contains 2.8 trillion parameters , while Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B contains 2.4 trillion parameters. Assuming BF16 weights at two bytes per parameter, their weight sizes are approximately 5.6 TB and 4.8 TB, respectively. Accounting for both the all-gather and broadcast stages gives an estimated logical payload of approximately twice the size of the model’s weights (Table 1). Model Size in bytes Refit payload estimate (all-gather+broadcast) Kimi K3 5.6 TB ≈11.2 TB Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B 4.8 TB ≈9.6 TB Table 1. Two-stage logical payload estimate assuming BF16 weights For today’s largest open weight models, the communication payload already reaches around 10 TB per refit, which must be performed at every training step. As LLMs continue to scale, the overhead associated with this large payload will become even more significant. As a result, a more sophisticated approach is needed to perform weight refit that reduces the actual payload size while properly accounting for diverse weight layouts. Reformulating refit as a DTensor-to-DTensor transfer problem To overcome these limitations, start from the principle that refit should transfer only the theoretical minimum amount of weight data. However, achieving this presents several challenges. Training and inference instances can use different parallelism configurations and GPU counts, producing different shard boundaries. A destination shard may therefore need to be assembled from portions of several source shards, and vice versa. Replication further complicates the mapping since the same weights may be available from multiple source GPUs or required by multiple destination GPUs. It is nontrivial to determine which source GPUs should send which tensor regions to each destination while achieving high performance across all possible configurations. The key to addressing this challenge is to identify the right abstraction for this unique communication pattern. The team turned to the existing PyTorch distributed tensor (DTensor) abstraction, which is designed to represent tensors that are sharded or replicated across GPUs under different forms of data and model parallelism. The key insight is that weight refit can be reformulated as resharding a DTensor from the training layout to the inference layout, regardless of the parallelism configurations used by the two instances. A DTensor layout is described by the tensor’s global shape, a device mesh specifying the logical arrangement of GPUs, and placements specifying how the tensor is sharded or replicated across that mesh. Refit can use the source description to specify where the updated weights reside and the destination description to specify which weights each inference GPU needs. For example, consider an 8 x 8 weight matrix split by rows across two training GPUs and by columns across four inference GPUs. Assuming the tensor is sharded in the row dimension on the training GPUs and sharded in the column dimension on the inference GPUs, each training GPU holds a 4 x 8 shard, while each inference GPU needs an 8 x 2 shard. Each destination can obtain its required shard by receiving a 4 x 2 region from each source. These regions follow directly from the overlap between the source and destination shards, as illustrated in Figure 1. Figure 1. Direct shard-to-shard transfer of an 8 x 8 tensor from two training GPUs to four inference GPUs. The pattern can be cleanly abstracted as a DTensor-to-DTensor reshard As the figure shows, any kind of sharded tensor can be easily represented as a DTensor format, and the refit can be redefined as a DTensor-to-DTensor reshard problem. This finding provides the foundation for the Reshard collective. Reshard collective communication for DTensor-to-DTensor transfers Reshard is a new type of collective communication call for arbitrary DTensor-to-DTensor transfers. Like all-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather, broadcast, and so on, reshard defines a communication pattern that applications can invoke as one operation. It transfers the values of a logical tensor from its source distribution into its destination distribution. A Reshard call can be specified simply by the source and destination DTensor descriptions. This abstraction not only simplifies the refit problem, but also encapsulates the communication logic in a library, allowing the underlying algorithms to evolve and improve independently of the application. NCCL M2N Reshard is open source, provided to the community as the first reference implementation of the Reshard collective. Built on NCCL, this implementation transfers a tensor distributed across M source GPUs into the layout required by N destination GPUs. In RL refit, the training GPUs form the source group and the inference GPUs form the destination group. Figure 2 shows how this implementation accepts the layout descriptions and local buffers to carry out the Reshard operation. Figure 2. The nccl.m2n.reshard example that transfers a tensor sharded across four training GPUs (TP4) into replicas on four inference GPUs (DP4) How NCCL M2N Reshard unlocks maximum network bandwidth NCCL M2N Reshard first derives the exact intersections between source and destination shards, then maps those transfers onto the physical GPU network topology. Instead of sending every source contribution independently to every destination replica, NCCL M2N groups replicas by NVIDIA NVLink domain.

title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
abstract: When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator. This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach. Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation. This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did. One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components , the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned. If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices. Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not. Use multi-model endpoints – These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic. But models share the device without isolation, so a heavy request for one model affects the others. A model that isn’t loaded also pays a load penalty on first use. Move to self-managed Kubernetes – This is where customers who need real GPU partitioning have gone. MIG works there, but you take on driver versioning, partition configuration, a device plugin, scheduling, and keeping it all consistent across a fleet. That’s a lot of work for a hardware capability your instances already have. NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give: Partitioning has boundaries worth knowing up front. The maximum number of partitions depends on the accelerator and never exceeds seven. MIG itself only allows a layout to change while its partitions are idle, and on SageMaker AI that means choosing a layout when you create the endpoint. A model that needs more than one GPU still needs whole devices. Within those boundaries, you get the isolation of separate GPUs without dedicating one to each model. Until now, getting MIG meant running the Kubernetes stack yourself. GPU partitioning on Amazon SageMaker AI removes that step: you pick a partition profile for your model, and SageMaker AI handles GPU configuration, placement and scaling. You get hardware-isolated GPU sharing on a managed endpoint, without having to run the platform underneath it. Salesforce has been part of this work from the start, helping define the requirements and validating the initial implementation. “NVIDIA MIG partitions a single GPU into multiple isolated instances, each with dedicated compute and memory resources. Salesforce sees this as an important capability because many inference workloads do not require an entire GPU. MIG would allow us to consolidate workloads safely, significantly improve GPU utilization, reduce inference costs, and maintain predictable performance and strong isolation. This capability would help us scale AI Inference more efficiently across different use cases. Salesforce has helped define requirements, validated the initial solution. We are now preparing to validate the solution with representative production workload and demonstrate strong customer demand with AWS. We believe MIG support would deliver meaningful technical and business value for enterprise customers.” — Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce GPU partitioning adds two optional fields to API calls you already make. There are no new API operations, no new resource types, and no new AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) actions, and an endpoint that omits both fields behaves exactly as it does today. AcceleratorPartitionLayouts goes on a production variant in CreateEndpointConfig and declares how each accelerator is divided: An A100 has seven compute slices to divide. The preceding layout uses all seven, so each of the eight A100s on the p4d instance carries three partitions and the endpoint provides 24, eight of each type. The carve applies uniformly. One layout entry describes how one accelerator is divided, and every accelerator on every instance in the variant is divided the same way. The list isn’t positional, so an entry doesn’t map to a specific GPU. AcceleratorPartitionType goes on an inference component and selects which partition the model runs on: Each component copy occupies one partition of the requested type. With eight partitions of each type on the instance, raising CopyCount places additional copies on free partitions. This is useful for a small model serving high concurrency, where a single process leaves the GPU waiting on requests. NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired is always 1 here. With a partition type set it means one partition rather than one accelerator. NumberOfCpuCoresRequired and MinMemoryRequiredInMb still describe host CPU and host memory, because GPU memory comes from the partition type. Invocation doesn’t change. InvokeEndpoint addresses a model by inference component name, and the partition it occupies never appears in the request. Partitioning happens while the endpoint is provisioned. When it reaches InService every accelerator is carved and the partitions are empty, which is a valid state as components land on them afterward. In our testing, carving accelerators added roughly 17 seconds to provisioning. The rest of the time is the usual instance launch and container pull. The profiles available to you are a property of the GPU, so start by finding out which GPU your instance type carries and look it up in NVIDIA’s supported MIG profiles , which is the authority on the full profile set and the combinations valid on one device. Read the profile name as compute units followed by GPU memory: mig-3g.40gb takes three compute units and 40 GB. The granularity column is what limits a layout. An A100 and an H100 divide into sevenths on compute and eighths on memory, while G7 divides into halves and G7e into quarters. Profile names differ between GPUs even where the slice counts match, so don’t carry a layout from one instance family to another without checking it against this table. Within those limits you have real choice. On a P4d or P5 you can carve seven of the smallest profile, or two 3g partitions, or the 4g plus 2g plus 1g layout used in the earlier example, or take the whole device as one. On a G7e you can take four of the smallest, or two 1g beside a 2g, or two 2g, or one whole device.

title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick
abstract: Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user. Take the user who says “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When? , What? , Who? , and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it. Figure 1: How triggers, agents, and capabilities relate, with learning feeding back from the session runtime A trigger starts the work and carries the task ( When and What ), an agent takes it on ( Who ) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task ( How ). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more. Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task. The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop). We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor . It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things: Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform. A consequence of this definition is that a user request “ I want an agent that monitors my Slack and sends a digest every morning ” is usually a trigger added to an existing agent , not a new agent or workflow. With this framing, we can merge chat, scheduled, and “autonomous” agents into one actor that you can converse with, schedule, and that can orchestrate and inspect its own past work. Capabilities are How an agent acts, spanning a spectrum from fully agentic to fully deterministic. That axis is really a confidence contract : how much latitude the agent keeps versus how much the user fixes in advance. Tools are atomic operations with a typed schema: send an email, query a database, read a file. Whether a local function, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, or another agent behind a protocol boundary, the caller sees the same interface: name, description, parameters, result. Skills are structured guidance with room for judgment: instructions bundled with resources (templates, scripts, examples) that describe an approach rather than a rigid sequence. They load through progressive disclosure , so the agent sees only names and short descriptions until one becomes relevant, then reads the full instructions in. A skill can therefore bundle arbitrary depth of expertise without a constant cost. Workflows are deterministic coordination: declared steps, control flow, branching, and error handling that execute in fixed order, with decision logic in code rather than model inference. Think of a purchase-approval route: budget check, manager sign-off, then finance, each recorded. The route is fixed, but the judgment inside a step is still the agent’s. Figure 2: Skills versus workflows, which differ in whether the agent or the code decides the step order A natural question arises: if models keep improving, won’t skills and workflows become unnecessary? We don’t think so, because each holds value independent of model capability. Skills are the unit for capturing, versioning, and sharing institutional expertise, while workflows deliver auditability, step-wise visibility, and deterministic multi-service coordination. Nor are they fixed: a well-understood skill can tighten into a workflow ( crystallization ), a workflow that keeps hitting edge cases can loosen back into a skill ( dissolution ). This is done in Quick through our continuous learning framework, which we will describe in a future post. Return to “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Because these primitives compose, the same request can be met several valid ways: All three produce a daily digest on a schedule. What differs is the confidence contract. A user who trusts the agent wants the first, one burned by inconsistency the second, one running a compliance-sensitive process the third. Learning shifts that trajectory over time. A task that starts as one sentence (“ check my email for urgent items ”) accumulates domain-bound learnings: effective queries, preferred formatting, and which senders matter. The tenth run is markedly better, with no one encoding that by hand. The right design is the simplest option that meets the user’s confidence requirement, with a path to graduate through autonomous learning when they need more. The value of this agentic primitive taxonomy is that four plain questions, When , What , Who , and How , are enough to place any piece of agentic work, from a one-line chat request to a scheduled, compliance-grade process. Sharing one vocabulary lets builders reason about the system and lets the product hide complexity. Best of all, the user never has to learn any of it. They say what they want, and the system assembles the appropriate primitives to do their job. Next in the series: the agentic operating system that builds on these primitives and powers Amazon Quick.

title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
abstract: Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort. Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync. In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment. Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model. Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table. We established four requirements: The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge-base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable. A metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, storing schema descriptions, column-level semantics, and table relationships that the AI agent references when generating SQL. Because the agent derives schema knowledge from the catalog at query time, there is no need to hardcode table structures or redeploy when schemas change. The knowledge-base refresh layer keeps that catalog current, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives. The following sections describe each layer in detail. The following diagram shows the request flow from user query to data layer across all four layers. A user submits a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53 for DNS and reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet, configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer routes to Amazon Cognito, which authenticates the user and enriches the request. Authenticated traffic then enters the private subnet, where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate. This layer handles session state in Amazon DynamoDB and forwards requests through an internal Application Load Balancer to the MCP server layer, also on Amazon ECS Fargate. In the MCP server layer, an AI agent powered by Amazon Bedrock orchestrates tools built with FastMCP (a Python framework for building MCP servers). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to every model interaction. On the right, the data layer holds the tool backends. Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift run SQL queries against the data lake, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handles semantic search. Data ingestion into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the knowledge bases is handled by AWS Lambda. Each layer is described in detail in the sections that follow. Figure 1: Request flow through the serverless MCP server, from client applications to the data layer A request flows from the client application through Amazon Route 53 for DNS resolution to an Application Load Balancer configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF . The load balancer forwards traffic to the Amazon ECS Fargate client service, which integrates with Amazon Cognito for JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication and Amazon DynamoDB for session storage. A context mapping configuration drives this enrichment, scoping each query to only the relevant tables. In our testing, this scoping keeps end-to-end interaction latency in the 15–20 second range. The following example shows a context mapping configuration: When a context specifies tables, the MCP server narrows its search of the metadata catalog to those tables, reducing noise and improving SQL generation accuracy. Adding a new business domain requires only adding an entry to this mapping. The MCP server runs on its own ECS Fargate cluster, isolated from the client layer. Requests reach it through Amazon Route 53 and an internal Application Load Balancer in a private subnet. The server handles full orchestration including query analysis, tool selection, execution, and response generation. Through the MCP protocol endpoint ( /mcp ), a FastMCP-powered JSON-RPC interface, external MCP-compatible clients such as Amazon Q Developer or IDE extensions can discover and invoke tools directly. Fargate tasks are stateless with conversation state persisted in DynamoDB, so tasks can be replaced or scaled without data loss. When a request arrives, the agent retrieves session history, analyzes user intent using Amazon Bedrock, discovers and invokes appropriate tools, and streams results back to the user. Each tool is registered with FastMCP and discoverable at runtime: The Athena query tools are the primary interface to the data lake. The agent first queries the metadata catalog to understand available schemas, generates an optimized SQL query through Amazon Bedrock, validates and auto-corrects the SQL for Athena compatibility, then executes it. Results flow back to the orchestrating agent for natural language synthesis. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to all LLM interactions and is designed to filter harmful content, enforce grounding checks, and help block prompt injection attempts. These guardrails operate as production controls at the MCP server layer, so every connected agent benefits from the same content safety policies regardless of how it connects. The Athena query tools enforce SELECT -only queries, rejecting write operations at the tool level before they reach the data lake. The entire system is built around configuration-driven extensibility. Adding a new dataset requires a metadata JSON file describing the table and an optional context mapping entry. The file captures the table’s schema, business context, and column-level semantics. It serves as the single source of truth that the AI agent uses to understand and query the dataset: The business_description_for_the_table field carries engine-specific query hints, such as “always use date() to wrap string literals,” that reduce SQL validation failures. The column_details field pairs each column_name [type] with a natural language description and sample values, giving the agent both schema awareness and business semantics. The sample_values field matters for accurate WHERE clause generation because the agent learns real data patterns, for instance that warehouse_id holds codes like FC-EAST-07 rather than spelled-out names like “East region facility.

title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
abstract: In Part 1 , you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server. The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools: In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant. The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions. Figure 1: The Part 1 solution with AgentCore Gateway, Policy, and Observability, a second agent on Amazon EKS, and the audit path, with numbers matching the steps that follow The reporting agent, agent B, runs on Amazon EKS and follows the same path through its own Gateway. In addition to the Part 1 solution, you need the following: The additions take about 90 minutes. The EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus nodes and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode management fee, and the AgentCore features charge for what you use. See Amazon EKS pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . As in Part 1, the base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain on GitHub, and you can build the Part 2 additions on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer works like the runtime authorizer from Part 1. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, its audience is the custom authorization server, and allowedClients pins it to one agent: Figure 2 shows the resulting inbound authorizer. Figure 2: The Gateway accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to the agent for the resource’s authorization server Each MCP server becomes a Gateway target whose outbound authorization uses TOKEN_EXCHANGE through the Part 1 credential provider, so the Gateway performs the second exchange: Figure 3 shows a target configured this way. Figure 3: The task manager target redeems the ID-JAG through the Part 1 credential provider Three details matter here. First, as in Part 1, the target’s scopes must equal the ID-JAG’s. Second, give each target a static tool schema ( listingMode set to DEFAULT with an inline mcpToolSchema ), so the tool names your Cedar policies reference are fixed when you write them. In our tests, policies that name tools also couldn’t attach to dynamically listed targets. Third, the Gateway pages tools/list by target, so your client must follow the pagination cursor, or tools from later targets disappear. AgentCore Identity keeps the token from the Gateway’s exchange, so one single-use ID-JAG serves every tool call in a session. In our tests, it also opened a second session within its 5-minute life. Because a credential provider authenticates as one Okta agent, give each agent its own Gateway and provider. Sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain takes a different route, in which a Gateway interceptor performs both exchanges itself. Attach a Policy in AgentCore engine to the Gateway in ENFORCE mode, and write permit-only policies. Cedar exposes JWT claims as tags. A policy that reads a missing tag errors and is skipped. A skipped permit grants nothing, so default deny holds, but a skipped forbid blocks nothing. Guard each tag with hasTag : The scope tag holds the ID-JAG’s space-separated scope claim, so the four conditions match xaa:write only as a whole entry. A scope such as xaa:write-admin doesn’t match. A matching policy, written the same way, permits the read tools with xaa:read . Check that every policy is ACTIVE before you attach the engine: an engine whose policies failed to create leaves the Gateway denying every call. Cedar binds tools to the agent and its delegated scope, and the MCP server still decides each user’s authority from the groups claim, as in Part 1. Agent A now forwards its inbound ID-JAG to the Gateway instead of calling AgentCore Identity itself: Remove the Part 1 AgentCore Identity statements from the agent’s execution role. That’s the only change to the role, which now holds no token-exchange or secret permissions, because the Gateway’s role holds the permission to exchange tokens. Keep allowedClients on the runtime’s authorizer. Our second agent, a reporting agent, runs the same code on Amazon EKS with its own Okta registration. Its resource connection allows only xaa:read , and it has its own Gateway and credential provider. EKS Pod Identity gives the pod an IAM role that can invoke models and write its own logs and traces, and nothing else. The AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK exports its traces. The agents-on-eks sample shows the Pod Identity setup. Outside AgentCore runtime, no authorizer sits in front of the pod, so the agent validates the ID-JAG before a model call. It checks the signature, issuer, audience, token type oauth-id-jag+jwt , expiry, and that client_id is its own. If you kept the Part 1 agent check in the MCP servers, add agent B’s client ID to REGISTERED_AGENTS . Two settings tripped us up. The EKS Auto Mode general-purpose node pool runs only amd64, so build multi-architecture images. And the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, binds to localhost unless you set DOCKER_CONTAINER=true . The spans in this section are AgentCore Observability , the component in Figure 1 that sits between the agents and CloudWatch. Runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Policy emit OpenTelemetry spans for each hop without code changes, after you turn on Transaction Search and trace delivery. Your own services add theirs with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). CloudWatch Transaction Search collects them, the AgentCore console reads them as agent traces, and Amazon CloudWatch Omni reads the same spans as traces.default , which is what lets one query put them beside Okta’s events. One tool call therefore produces this chain of spans, each naming the control that made a decision: Okta’s System Log is the one record AWS can’t emit, so you bring it in. Figure 4 shows both paths meeting in Omni. Figure 4: The audit path, where spans and Okta’s System Log reach CloudWatch and one Omni query joins them One query then joins each ID-JAG grant to the decisions it led to: For Alice, the result shows Okta granting the task agent xaa:read xaa:write for her, then the MCP server denying her create_task 16.7 seconds later and allowing list_tasks after that, as Figure 5 shows.

title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
abstract: An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end. In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime. Figure 1: Solution architecture, with numbers matching the steps that follow Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this: Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes. Figure 2: The three-token chain and the check each party makes, with the step 4 workload access token staying inside AWS To follow along, you need the following: The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it. Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard. Figure 3: The task agent’s resource connection in Okta, limited to the xaa:read and xaa:write scopes Okta’s Cross App Access guide covers the console steps, and the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain scripts the authorization server and its JWT bearer policy. The BFF then requests the ID-JAG, authenticated as the agent: The AWS sample 06-okta-xaa sends the same request in Python ( agent/xaa_client.py ). The BFF authenticates as the agent, so store the agent’s client secret in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in code or configuration files. AgentCore Identity holds three things for this solution, and your agent code doesn’t see the client secret or call Okta’s token endpoint: The credential provider performs the second exchange. Point it at the custom authorization server, authenticate it as the AI agent, and set the on-behalf-of grant to JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT , which AgentCore Identity sends as jwt-bearer with the ID-JAG as the assertion: Okta binds both exchanges to the client named in the ID-JAG, so each Okta agent needs its own provider: when we redeemed one agent’s ID-JAG as another, Okta refused with “The ‘client_id’ in the JWT Bearer Grant must match the ‘client_id’ used to authenticate the client.” AgentCore Identity keeps the secret in a service-managed AWS Secrets Manager secret, which you rotate with update-oauth2-credential-provider . If your team already manages the client secret in Secrets Manager, you can reference that secret’s ARN instead. AgentCore Identity reads the client secret from it, so you can rotate the secret without updating the provider (see Reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity ). To avoid a shared secret, authenticate with a private key instead. See Authenticate with Private Key JWT using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity . Figure 4 shows the provider in the AgentCore console. Figure 4: The credential provider authenticating as the agent with the JWT authorization grant AgentCore runtime creates and manages a workload identity for each agent runtime. When a request passes the runtime’s JWT authorizer, the runtime gets a workload access token for that workload identity and the inbound token’s issuer and subject, and passes it to your code. AgentCore Identity then uses the ID-JAG behind it as the assertion for the exchange. The AgentCore Python SDK keeps the workload access token in BedrockAgentCoreContext , not in the request headers that your entrypoint receives. Our first version looked for it in the headers, found nothing, and fell back to its own GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT call with a second workload identity, on all 21 requests we checked. Read it from the context instead: AgentCore Identity keeps the access token in its token vault for the rest of the request. Across 10 requests, the agent’s first call redeemed the ID-JAG in about half a second (see the latency table in Validate the results), and the second, for the other MCP server, returned the same token in a median of 58 milliseconds without redeeming the single-use ID-JAG again. A new ID-JAG for the same user got a new token, so each request reflects Okta’s latest decision. The sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain reads the workload access token the same way ( agent/agent.py ). AgentCore Identity doesn’t bind workload identities to credential providers in the same account. The agent’s IAM role does, so scope it to the agent’s own workload identity and provider, and to that provider’s secret: Take the workload identity’s name from workloadIdentityDetails in GetAgentRuntime , and the provider’s ARN from credentialProviderArn : the segment is oauth2credentialprovider , and with the hyphenated form every call failed with AccessDeniedException . The role needs no GetWorkloadAccessToken permission, because the runtime gets that token, not the agent. Our tests passed with only these two statements. Configure the agent runtime’s inbound authorizer to accept only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, and its audience is the resource’s custom authorization server. In agentcore.

title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds. This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries. Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks. Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors: Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks. Greenlight needed a system that could: Greenlight built Luna as a hierarchical multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture follows a tiered supervisor pattern that mirrors how human SOC teams operate. L1 handles volume, and L2 handles complexity. Figure 1: Luna’s tiered supervisor architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Tier 1 supervisor uses an advanced language model available through Amazon Bedrock running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The runtime uses private subnets and direct code deployment through a ZIP file and Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ). It handles initial triage of incoming cases by orchestrating more than 30 specialized agents: The Tier 1 supervisor receives cases through two paths: Amazon API Gateway, which exposes the Luna Queue API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, and Tines SOAR for automated alert ingestion. It determines which specialized agents to invoke based on alert type, synthesizes their findings, and renders a verdict. The median triage time for routine cases is single-digit seconds. Cases that exceed Tier 1’s confidence threshold escalate to a Tier 2 supervisor using an advanced foundation model on Amazon Bedrock with extended reasoning capabilities. This agent handles the 10 percent of cases that require multi-step reasoning: The Tier 2 supervisor runs on a scheduled basis, using Amazon EventBridge rate triggers and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) queue completions to batch-process escalated cases, and on demand for urgent Tier 1-escalated cases. Different teams engage Luna in different ways, so the application exposes three entry points. These range from fully automated alert ingestion to interactive, on-demand investigation. Each entry point maps to a persona and how their work arrives: The memory layer is built on AgentCore memory. This layer is what separates Luna from a stateless triage tool. It supports pattern recognition, deduplication, and continuous accuracy improvement. Stores recent events and resolution outcomes. When a new alert arrives, Luna checks: “Have I seen this pattern in the last 30 days? What was the verdict? Is this a known behavior that I should allowlist?” Concrete example: A Greenlight infrastructure role generates a specific access pattern every Tuesday at 3 AM for scheduled maintenance. Without memory, Luna would flag this every week. With episodic memory, Luna learned after the first resolution that this pattern is expected and auto-allowlists it. Persists semantic preferences and resolution templates beyond the 30-day window: A dedicated pipeline feeds resolution outcomes back into the system: This pipeline drove Luna’s autonomous resolution rate from 83 percent (Tier 1 only) to more than 90 percent (Tier 1, Tier 2, and learnings). Greenlight expanded Luna into financial risk assessment within two months of the SOC deployment. The architectural changes were minimal: new specialized agents and a risk-domain supervisor layered onto the existing infrastructure. When a Greenlight customer card appears on the dark web, Luna executes this workflow autonomously: Greenlight receives hundreds of breach card notifications daily. Luna processes each in seconds. A human analyst doing the same work, logging into Galileo, checking DynamoDB, opening Mixpanel, searching Zendesk, takes 15-30 minutes per card. The following table tracks Greenlight’s security operations on the metrics that matter most to the SOC. It compares three stages: manual triage before Luna, Tier 1 automation, and the full Tier 1 and Tier 2 system. Estimated analyst time avoided: Based on Greenlight’s case volume and manual handling-time measurements, processing 4,000 cases at 15–30 minutes each would require approximately 1,000–2,000 analyst hours per month. Greenlight reports that Luna autonomously resolves more than 90 percent of these cases, avoiding an estimated 900–1,800 hours of routine manual work each month. Analysts can focus instead on cases that require human judgment. The risk reduction comes from two factors: speed (seconds compared to minutes reduces the exposure window) and consistency (Luna applies the same triage logic at 3 AM on Saturday that it does at 10 AM on Tuesday, with no fatigue and no shortcuts).
