title: Where each U.S. state gets its tax revenue from
abstract:
How the 50 States Generate Their Tax Revenue Key Takeaways Property taxes are the largest individual tax category in 25 states, including Florida, Texas, and New York. Washington collects nearly half of its combined state and local tax revenue from general sales and gross receipts taxes. Delaware stands out for license taxes, reflecting its role as a legal home for businesses. From paychecks and purchases to homes and businesses, states rely on different combinations of taxes to fund public services. This graphic breaks down combined state and local tax revenue across all 50 states using 2024 government finance data from the U.S. Census Bureau . The percentages show each category’s share of tax collections, excluding federal taxes and funding such as federal grants. Property Taxes Lead in Half the Country Property taxes are the largest revenue source in half of U.S. states, with particularly high shares in New Hampshire (64.3%), Alaska (42.4%), and Texas (41.1%). General sales and gross receipts taxes lead in 16 states, while individual income taxes top the list in seven. The country’s largest states illustrate these differences. Individual income taxes dominate in California, while property taxes narrowly exceed general sales taxes in Florida and individual income taxes in New York. State Biggest Revenue Source in 2024 Share of Total Tax Revenue Alabama General sales taxes 32.3% Alaska Property taxes 42.4% Arizona General sales taxes 46.9% Arkansas General sales taxes 42.5% California Individual income taxes 30.7% Colorado Property taxes 33.6% Connecticut Property taxes 34.9% Delaware License taxes 33.0% Florida Property taxes 37.4% Georgia Property taxes 31.6% Hawaii General sales taxes 35.9% Idaho General sales taxes 28.5% Illinois Property taxes 33.4% Indiana General sales taxes 28.4% Iowa Property taxes 32.9% Kansas Property taxes 30.1% Kentucky Individual income taxes 28.0% Louisiana General sales taxes 39.1% Maine Property taxes 39.6% Maryland Individual income taxes 35.6% Massachusetts Property taxes 34.1% Michigan Property taxes 33.9% Minnesota Individual income taxes 27.5% Mississippi General sales taxes 34.5% Missouri Property taxes 28.8% Montana Property taxes 36.4% Nebraska Property taxes 33.3% Nevada General sales taxes 44.8% New Hampshire Property taxes 64.3% New Jersey Property taxes 40.5% New Mexico General sales taxes 33.7% New York Property taxes 28.8% North Carolina General sales taxes 29.0% North Dakota Other taxes 40.7% Ohio Property taxes 28.1% Oklahoma General sales taxes 33.4% Oregon Individual income taxes 34.2% Pennsylvania Individual income taxes 26.4% Rhode Island Property taxes 34.3% South Carolina Property taxes 29.0% South Dakota General sales taxes 43.3% Tennessee General sales taxes 47.8% Texas Property taxes 40.9% Utah General sales taxes 30.3% Vermont Property taxes 39.8% Virginia Property taxes 31.9% Washington General sales taxes 49.0% West Virginia Individual income taxes 23.2% Wisconsin Property taxes 31.0% Wyoming Property taxes 38.5% Including local governments makes a substantial difference. In Texas, for example, property taxes are collected by local tax authorities and support services such as schools, roads, and fire protection, even though the state government itself levies no property tax. These shares describe how governments raise money, rather than how much an individual household owes. A large property-tax share can reflect limited collections from other taxes as well as substantial property-tax revenue. How States Fund Services Without Taxing Wages Florida collects no individual income tax revenue, with property and general sales taxes together supplying about three-quarters of state and local tax collections. In Texas, those two categories account for nearly 79%, highlighting both states’ reliance on property and consumption taxes. New Hampshire takes that pattern further: property taxes generated 64.3% of tax revenue, the highest share nationwide. The state has no general sales tax and does not tax wages. Its small individual income tax share in 2024 reflects the interest and dividends tax, which was repealed effective in 2025. Sales-related collections also extend beyond the checkout counter. General sales taxes include taxes on business gross receipts, while selective sales taxes apply to particular products or activities, such as fuel, tobacco, and utilities. This helps explain why a state’s revenue mix can look different from the taxes shoppers encounter directly. Delaware and North Dakota: The Outliers Delaware’s largest revenue source is license taxes, accounting for roughly one-third of collections. This category includes corporate franchise licenses and related charges, giving it a much broader meaning than driver’s licenses or hunting permits. That revenue source connects to Delaware’s position in corporate America. In 2024, the state was the legal home of more than two million business entities and about two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies. Incorporation generates public revenue from businesses whose operations extend far beyond Delaware’s borders. North Dakota’s unusual mix reflects another economic advantage: natural resources. “Other taxes,” which include severance taxes on resource extraction, supplied 40.7% of collections. The state levies taxes on oil and gas production and oil extraction, linking part of its public finances to the value of energy produced within its borders. See 2026 salary purchasing power rankings and why U.S. wages stretch further than Canada’s. Published November 6, 2026 10:25 am By Dorothy Neufeld Where Does Your Salary Go the Furthest in 2026? Key Takeaways Kuwait ranks first in 2026, where average salaries buy the most goods and services at local prices. The U.S. ranks sixth, with salaries offering 26% more purchasing power than in Canada. Cuba ranks last, followed by Syria and Nigeria, where wages buy the least at local prices. A higher salary doesn’t always mean greater purchasing power. As housing, food, and other everyday expenses put pressure on household budgets, what matters is how much a paycheck can actually buy. This visualization uses data from Numbeo to compare salary purchasing power across 142 countries in 2026. The index measures average take-home salaries relative to local prices, using New York City as a benchmark of 100. title: Window Sweaters
abstract:
Window Sweaters for macOS A little Mac app I made to give my windows sweaters. 🧶
Knitted borders, colours inspired by your favourite apps, and a cosier desktop. window-sweaters-demo-github.mp4 See Window Sweaters in action on X → Get it You can just send this repo to your coding agent and ask it to install Window Sweaters for you: Install Window Sweaters on my Mac: https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters Or install it yourself with Homebrew : brew trust saragordic/tap
brew install --cask saragordic/tap/window-sweaters Then open Window Sweaters from your Applications folder. You can also grab the latest ZIP from Releases , unzip it, and drag Window Sweaters.app into Applications. If macOS blocks it, open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway after trying to launch it. The app isn't notarized by Apple yet. Apple's instructions explain this step. Make yourself cosy Click the yarn icon in your menu bar to change the style, pattern, border width, and stitch size. You can also pause the sweaters or quit from there. To leave an app bare, open Apps and untick it. Its windows lose their sweater straight away, everything else stays as it is, and it stays off until you tick it again, even after a restart. Only want sweaters on a few apps? Choose Turn Off for All Apps , then tick the ones you like. Apps you open later start off too. By App gives each app its own sweater. Zigzag gives them all a softer, matching cream zigzag in colours taken from their icons. Try both and see what you like. If macOS asks for Accessibility access, enable Window Sweaters in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility so it can follow which window is focused. The sweaters Custom sweaters for 37 apps, and counting! Almost 40 little colourways, with colours picked by hand. These are just a few of my favourites: Shown above in By App and Zigzag. Here’s everyone we’ve knitted for so far: Apple: Finder, Safari, Mail, Messages, Notes, Calendar, Reminders, Apple Music, Photos, Preview, Terminal. Work and notes: Notion, Paper, Granola, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Zoom. Coding and AI: Cursor, VS Code, Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Grok Bot, Ghostty. Design: Figma, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator. Microsoft Office: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook. More favourites: Spotify, WhatsApp, Google Chrome, Firefox, Telegram, Discord. See every sweater and its close-up stitches in the catalogue , or download the By App PDF . The 37 custom sweaters keep their hand-picked colours and patterns. Other apps borrow colours from their own icons, softened into yarn, and get a two-colour zigzag, picnic or twinkle sweater in By App mode. The pattern stays the same for each app. If an icon has no usable colour, the app keeps a stable colour chosen from its name. Icons are sampled locally in the background when needed. While the colour is being prepared, the border uses its usual fallback. Zigzag uses icon colours for every app, the 37 custom ones included, with a cream zigzag, or a deeper shade of the app’s colour on pale apps. Colours you set in apps.conf always win. Other shared patterns keep their own contrast yarns, with each app’s own base colour. A little work in progress I built this on my Mac and use it myself, but there are still rough edges. Borders hide while you resize a window and return when you're done. The app is built for macOS 13 or later, on Apple Silicon and Intel . I've tested it on Apple Silicon with macOS 26; older macOS versions and Intel Macs haven't had the same hands-on testing. It uses private macOS window APIs, so system updates may affect how it works. If something looks wrong, open an issue and tell me your macOS version, Mac model, and whether you're using another screen. Reproduction steps help a lot. Build it yourself You'll need Apple's Command Line Tools ( xcode-select --install ) and Python 3. git clone https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters.git cd window-sweaters
./scripts/build-app.sh
python3 scripts/install-local.py This builds outputs/Window Sweaters.app , installs it in ~/Applications , and opens it. The installer backs up any previous local installation before replacing it. Your own colourways If you'd like to experiment, edit these files and restart the app: ~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/apps.conf
~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/charts/ The folder still uses the app's original name so existing settings keep working. For example, an app rule looks like this: Claude = #D58561 atelier-claude Names match app-name prefixes, ignoring capitalisation; the longest match wins. You can also put your own PNG charts in the charts folder to replace built-in patterns. If you like setting things up from the command line, Window Sweaters also runs an optional shell script at startup, if you have one at ~/.config/window-sweaters/sweatersrc or ~/.sweatersrc . Taking it off Quit Window Sweaters from the yarn icon first. Then, if you installed it with Homebrew: brew uninstall --zap --cask window-sweaters --zap also removes your saved colourways. Leave it off to keep them for later. If you installed it by hand, drag Window Sweaters.app to the Trash, then delete these if you want everything gone: ~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders
~/Library/Preferences/local.knitborders.app.plist macOS remembers the Accessibility permission separately, so remove Window Sweaters from System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility too. Contributing make test # run the tests make catalogue # render the sweater collection make bench # benchmark the renderer See CONTRIBUTING.md for more details. Launch the live demo | Try Unleash Enterprise for free What is Unleash? Unleash is a powerful open-source solution for feature management. It streamlines your development workflow, accelerates software delivery, and empowers teams to control how and when they roll out new features to end users. With Unleash, you can deploy code to production in smaller, more manageable releases at your own pace. Feature flags in Unleash let you test your code with real production data, reducing the risk of negatively impacting your users' experience. It also enables your team to work on multiple features simultaneously without the need for separate feature branches. Unleash is the most popular open-source solution for feature flagging on GitHub. It supports 15 official client and server SDKs and over 15 community SDKs. You can even create your own SDK if you wish. Unleash is compatible with any language and framework. Get started with Unleash Set up Unleash To get started with Unleash, you can either explore Unleash Enterprise with a free trial or get started locally with our open-source solution. Unleash Enterprise To start with Unleash Enterprise, request a free trial . This gives you access to a hosted instance with unlimited projects and environments and features such as role-based access control , change requests , single sign-on , and SCIM for automatic user provisioning. Unleash Open Source To set up Unleash locally, you'll need git and docker installed on your machine. Execute the following commands: git clone git@github.com:Unleash/unleash.git cd unleash
docker compose up -d Then point your browser to localhost:4242 and log in using: username: admin password: unleash4all If you'd rather run the source code in this repo directly via Node.js, see the step-by-step instructions to get up and running in the contributing guide . Connect your SDK Find your preferred SDK in our list of official SDKs and import it into your project. Follow the setup guides for your specific SDK. If you use the docker compose file from the previous step, here's the configuration details you'll need to get going: For frontend SDKs, use: URL: http://localhost:4242/api/frontend/ clientKey : default:development.unleash-insecure-frontend-api-token For backend SDKs, use: Unleash API URL: http://localhost:4242/api/ API token: default:development.unleash-insecure-api-token If you use a different setup, your configuration details will most likely also be different. Check a feature flag Checking the state of a feature flag in your code is easy! The syntax will vary depending on your language, but all you need is a simple function call to check whether a flag is available. Here's how it might look in Java: if ( unleash . isEnabled ( "AwesomeFeature" )) { // do new, flashy thing } else { // do old, boring stuff } Try Unleash in the cloud Want to explore Unleash without setting it up locally? Here are two easy ways to see it in action. Live demo Open a running Unleash environment in your browser with no signup or setup required. This shared demo instance includes the core functionality so you can quickly get a feel for how Unleash works. → Launch the live demo Free Enterprise trial Get your own dedicated instance with a free 14-day cloud trial. This includes the full Unleash Enterprise feature set; ideal when evaluating Unleash for production use. → Start your free trial Deploying to a production server To self-host Unleash in a production environment, you need to deploy it to a persistent server. We provide guides for deploying to services like Heroku and DigitalOcean: For more advanced configurations options, check out our documentation on: Getting started with self-hosting Unleash configuration options Community and help We know that learning a new tool can be hard and time-consuming. We have a growing community that loves to help out. Please don't hesitate to reach out for help. 💬 Join Unleash on Slack if you want ask open questions about Unleash, feature toggling or discuss these topics in general. 💻 Create a GitHub issue if you have found a bug or have ideas on how to improve Unleash. 📚 Visit the documentation for more in-depth descriptions, how-to guides, and more. 📖 Learn more about the principles of building and scaling feature flag solutions. Contribute to Unleash Unleash is the largest open-source feature flag solution on GitHub. Building Unleash is a collaborative effort, and we owe a lot of gratitude to many smart and talented individuals. Building it together with the community ensures that we build a product that solves real problems for real people. We'd love to have your help too: Please feel free to open issues or provide pull requests. Check out the CONTRIBUTING.md file for contribution guidelines and the Unleash developer guide for tips on environment setup, running the tests, and running Unleash from source. Before a pull request can be merged, contributors must read and agree to the Unleash Contributor License Agreement . Contributors Documentation You can visit the Unleash documentation at https://docs.getunleash.io . As of 2 February 2026, the Unleash documentation source code lives in its own repository: Unleash/unleash-documentation . Canary releases / gradual rollouts Kill switches A/B testing 2 environments Organize feature flags using tags Out-of-the-box integrations with popular tools ( Slack , Microsoft Teams , Datadog ) + integrate with anything with webhooks Insights for managing technical debt and stale flags API-first: everything can be automated. title: Nvidia Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)
abstract:
NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure. NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and
operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its
own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management
plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and kubectl . Preview: NVKE is available as a preview. APIs, configuration and behavior
can change between releases, and we do not recommend NVKE for production
workloads. See Preview status and known limitations . Get started · Documentation · Contribute · Get help Getting started Your goal Start here What you get Evaluate without GPU hardware Local quickstart A development management plane and a workload cluster on simulated machines. No NVIDIA account is required. Install on your infrastructure Plan your installation The prerequisites and sequence for preparing nodes, bootstrapping a management cluster and installing its services. Build or contribute Build from source The NVKE binaries and the contributor development loop. The local quickstart runs on a Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64 , with at least 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of free memory and 100 GiB of free disk . It requires Docker,
virtual TPM support and the tools listed in the guide. Follow its setup through
workload-cluster creation and confirm the cluster's nodes report Ready .
On macOS, use the local site guide , which runs
the evaluation inside a Colima virtual machine. For a real installation, you supply the machines, networking, node images and
registries, and configure access to NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo) . NICo is
the sole compatible infrastructure provider at preview. The platform and version reference lists
validated combinations and pinned dependencies. What NVKE does Creates independent workload clusters. Request clusters through the NVKE
API or nvkectl ; NVKE provisions machines through NICo and forms Kubernetes
clusters with their own control planes. Manages workload cluster lifecycle. Create, scale and delete node pools,
upgrade Kubernetes and replace nodes. See the node pool guide for the manual steps and preview limits on replacement and upgrades. Establishes node identity. Nodes attest through SPIFFE/SPIRE using their
TPM before receiving join credentials. Encryption of etcd data is available
per cluster. Connects builds to deployment. Its companion project, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) ,
builds node images and NVKE components from pinned inputs. NVKE deploys those
artifacts; NVKR owns their build and release evidence. The preview needs explicit operator configuration: API authentication is off
and the API uses plain HTTP after installation. Configure API authentication and protected access before admitting callers. The management cluster does not upgrade, scale or
replace itself, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup/restore
procedure. FDE node images are for evaluation and provide no data-at-rest
confidentiality. Read the known limitations before choosing an evaluation or installation path. Overview The diagram shows the NVKE product family, how it sits on NICo and your GPU machines, and which components talk to each other. NVKE is not a Kubernetes distribution and not a Cluster API flavour. It is a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters : a throwaway seed cluster
stands up a management cluster, and the management plane on
it then provisions and lifecycle-manages many isolated workload clusters
on demand. An installation has two kinds of Kubernetes cluster: The management cluster runs the NVKE management plane and infrastructure
controllers. nvkectl forms it using a temporary seed cluster; installing the
management-plane services is a separate step. Workload clusters run customer applications. The management plane creates

title: MoofTCP – A modern replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs
abstract:
MoofTCP A modern, memory-lean replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs running System 6. MoofTCP is a drop-in replacement for Apple's MacTCP. Programs written for MacTCP run on it unchanged, but
underneath it is a fresh TCP/IP stack written from scratch in portable C, with its own control panel, installer
and DHCP client. It was built for a Mac Classic with 4 MB of RAM, so every byte counts. Why? MacTCP is wonderful, but it is old, and on a 4 MB Mac Classic with a SCSI Wi-Fi/Ethernet adapter like
BlueSCSI it can be slow to answer, hungry for memory, and awkward to set up. MoofTCP aims, in this order, for: Reliability. No hangs, no leaks, no surprises when apps quit. Low latency for interactive use, like typing in a telnet session. Throughput , for handling quasi-modern use cases. ...all while using no more resident memory than MacTCP does . Features Drop-in compatible. Implements the MacTCP .IPP driver interface (TCP, UDP, ICMP echo) and the dnrp name resolver. Your existing MacTCP programs just work. DHCP or a fixed address. Pick either in the control panel. Don't need to manage static IP anymore. MoofTCP Lite. A build without DHCP that saves about 5 KB of system memory, for tight machines. One
installer holds both; a checkbox picks which one. A friendly installer. It moves MacTCP's files aside, installs MoofTCP, and its Remove button puts
everything back exactly as it was. An interrupted install repairs itself. MultiFinder-aware. Quitting an app that had connections open cleans up after it. Built-in diagnostics. An optional in-memory log and a small MoofDiag tool for bug reports. A portable core. The TCP/IP stack in core/ has no malloc and no global state, and is tested on the
desktop with sanitizers and fuzzers. Screenshots Installer MoofTCP Lite panel Quick start Download MoofTCP-1.0.dsk , MoofTCP-1.0.hqx or MoofTCP-1.0.sit from the Releases page and get it onto your Mac (a BlueSCSI shared folder works well). Open MoofTCP Installer , leave Lite version (no DHCP) unticked, and click Install . Restart the Mac. Open Control Panels, MoofTCP , enter your IP address, mask, router and DNS server (or tick Get the address by DHCP ), and save. Restart again. You're online. To go back to MacTCP, run the installer and click Remove . The Read Me file in the release has the
details, including how to switch between MoofTCP and MoofTCP Lite. StuffIt Lite 3.6 is tested as working for expanding the .hqx packages. What you need A 68k Mac with System 6.0.8 (the version it was tested on). Please report back if it works on other versions! An Ethernet adapter that provides the .ENET0 driver, such as a BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT . MoofTCP
does not include an Ethernet driver. Compatibility Tested on a real Mac Classic (System 6.0.8, 4 MB, BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT) and in the Snow emulator. Program Result Flynn (telnet terminal) Works, real Mac and emulator Wikipedia Reader Works, real Mac and emulator MacTCP Watcher Works in the emulator NCSA Telnet Works in the emulator Fetch (FTP) Works in the emulator TurboGopher Works in the emulator Eudora Starts; mail was not tried Have a program that doesn't work? Please open an issue (see below). Memory MoofTCP MoofTCP Lite Driver code 95,623 bytes 90,722 bytes Free system heap after first open (real Mac Classic, single Finder, full build) about 30.7 KB n/a MultiFinder grows the system heap on demand, so free memory varies more there. Something went wrong? MoofTCP keeps a small diagnostic log in memory. If a program misbehaves but the Mac keeps running, run MoofDiag right away (it is in the release's diagnostic tools download), and open an issue with the MoofDiag.out file it writes next to itself, plus a note about what you were doing. Feel free to ask your LLM
to analyze the codebase and the diagnostic output as well and to submit fix PRs. Known limitations No IPv6. Tested only with the DaynaPORT Ethernet driver on System 6.0.8. DHCP is basic: no lease RELEASE, no INIT-REBOOT and no address-conflict probe. While it runs, programs cannot
use UDP port 68. With no DHCP server, the first open waits about 10 seconds and then fails. Building from source You only need Docker. The pinned Retro68 cross-compiler image is pulled
automatically. scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP # the MoofTCP file -> build-mac/moof/ MT_LITE=1 scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP # MoofTCP Lite -> build-mac-lite/ scripts/release.sh --force 1.0 # one installer with both -> dist/MoofTCP-1.0.{dsk,hqx,sit} release.sh also needs hfsutils, macutils, unar, gcc and Python 3. Running the tests The portable core and the glue logic are tested on your desktop with gcc and CMake (AddressSanitizer and
UBSan are on by default): cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
cmake -S . -B build-lite -DMT_NO_DHCP=ON # the Lite configuration The emulator tests (Snow) need Apple system software and the BlueSCSI DaynaPORT image. Those are not in this
repository and you must supply them yourself; the scripts in scripts/ ( setup-home.sh , golden-stage.sh ) show
what is expected. Project layout core/ portable TCP/IP stack (no malloc, no globals), host-tested
mac/ Mac glue: .IPP driver, INIT, resolver, control panel, installer, diagnostic apps
tests/ host tests (ctest), including fuzzers
scripts/ build, release, emulator and hardware-session scripts
tools/ pinned tool versions; tools/sit is a small StuffIt-format writer Contributing Bug reports, compatibility reports ("program X does/doesn't work") and pull requests are welcome. For code
changes, please read CONTRIBUTING.md and run the host tests first (see above). CLAUDE.md is a
detailed map of the code and its rules. Security problems: see SECURITY.md . Credits Retro68 for the 68k cross-compiler. Snow for the Mac emulator the tests run in. BlueSCSI and DaynaPORT for the network hardware this was built around. Claude Code was used to develop this project, with human planning and testing. TODO More comprehensive bake-in testing on real hardware as we use it Remake Daynaport similarly (stay tuned for MoofPort ) Review the BlueSCSI codebase for opportunities to integrate more tightly for better performance There is potential for further algorithm optimization for added performance on smaller or older systems. License MIT . "MacTCP" and "StuffIt" are trademarks of their owners and are used here only to describe
compatibility. MoofTCP contains no Apple or third-party code; building it uses Apple's interfaces as shipped in
the Retro68 toolchain.

title: Tencent launches Hy4
abstract:
Tencent today announced the release of Tencent Hy4, its latest-generation large language model, marking a significant leap in performance and capabilities that now ranks it among the world’s leading open-source AI models. Tencent Hy plans to release model weights and system cards in the coming days, reinforcing its commitment to responsible open-source AI development, with a focus on cybersecurity and biological safety. The new model also introduces visual understanding capabilities for the first time, alongside major improvements in instruction following, long-context comprehension and long-horizon agentic tasks, delivering stronger overall performance across a diverse set of applications. Through advanced visual understanding, reasoning, and tool-calling capabilities, Hy4 now supports a broader range of tasks, including fine-grained image processing, complex chart analysis, and mathematical visual reasoning. Additionally, Hy4 introduces computer-use capabilities for the first time, enabling it to interact with both command-line interfaces and graphical user interfaces to perform a wide range of work and everyday tasks. The model has undergone specialized training on professional software such as Blender and CAD, significantly enhancing its ability to plan and execute long-horizon and sophisticated tasks. Deep Model-Product Co-Design Unlocks New Opportunities for Real-World Productivity Leveraging significant advances in its foundational capabilities and deep model-product co-design, Hy4 unlocks a broader range of real-world productivity scenarios: Office Productivity & Collaboration : Hy4 has significantly enhanced the user experience on Tencent WorkBuddy. Evaluation benchmarks on WorkBuddy show an average performance score of 83.18 and a pass rate of 96.15 percent, with Hy4 ranking first place in nine out of twelve scenarios within the mainland Chinese market. In practical use, Hy4 balances efficiency and effectiveness for visual creative tasks, 3D scene construction, and web development. Furthermore, it delivers marked improvements in document presentation, stability, and usability for human-AI collaborative tasks on WorkBuddy. Leveraging enhanced in-context learning capabilities, Hy4 excels at understanding complex information from diverse sources. Integrated with WeCom via WorkBuddy, Hy4 connects with daily workflow data across chats, emails, documents, calendars, and meetings. When managing multiple projects simultaneously, Hy4 automatically tracks project history and recent developments. It identifies outstanding tasks, flags upcoming meetings that require preparation, and monitors approaching deadlines, helping users prioritize effectively and stay aligned on important follow-ups. In addition, new team collaboration capabilities powered by Hy4 will be introduced with the upcoming release of WorkBuddy’s “Projects” feature. Hy4 has also been optimized for professional financial analysis. By training on thousands of specialized workspaces and tens of thousands of high-quality tasks derived from real-world scenarios, the model gains a deep understanding of expert workflows in fund research, securities analysis, and quantitative investment strategies. In a rigorous blind evaluation conducted by the Tencent Hy team in partnership with Tencent Financial Technology, Hy4 emerged as the top-performing open-source model. The assessment involved 213 financial professionals, including 153 experts from leading external institutions, approximately 70 percent of whom possessed more than five years of industry experience. Based on performance across 579 real-world financial tasks, Hy4 achieved the highest overall performance score. Evaluation scores: Hy4 (3.04), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (2.97), Kimi K3.1 Pro (2.68), and GLM-5.3 (2.68). In addition, Hy4 achieved a 12.03 percentage-point improvement over Hy4 Preview in the internal Investment Research Agent Benchmark (iRaB) evaluation conducted by financial AI company Rabyte. To enhance the model’s real-world applicability across financial and other workplace scenarios, Tencent Hy has also introduced targeted search optimisation that focuses on retrieving up-to-date information, integrating multiple information sources, and verifying factual consistency. In internal evaluations, Hy4 reduced its hallucination rate from 12.95% in the Hy4 Preview to 7.2%, while errors caused by unsupported assumptions fell from 23.1% to 5.6%. Frontend & Game Development: Hy4 is optimized for high-complexity tasks, including intricate business logic, state management, front-end and back-end orchestration. This ensures that generated interfaces are not only visually polished but also fully functional. Furthermore, through collaboration with Tencent Interactive Entertainment Group (IEG) professional developers, Hy4 has significantly advanced its game development capabilities. By deeply integrating with major engines like Unreal Engine (UE), Unity, and Godot, the model now supports complex game logic and multiplayer implementations. Compared to Hy4 Preview, Hy4 improved by 19.1 percent in GameDev and 9.8 percent in GameLogic benchmarks. Scientific Research: Hy4 combines advanced reasoning, scientific programming, and long-horizon task execution to support complex, end-to-end research workflows. Validated with TenureTrail, which assessed 123 executable tasks across seven disciplines, the model demonstrated superior performance in mathematical construction, physical modeling, environmental and earth sciences, systems engineering, and socio-economic decision-making. Hy4 is advancing into the next stage of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to further enhance its model research and development capabilities. Leveraging the Hyra 2.0 harness, Hy4 optimized the pre-training infrastructure for smaller models sharing the same architecture. Additionally, the Hy team has open-sourced two foundational models developed with Hy4 and Hyra 2.0 for single-cell representations (HyCell) and the physics fields (HyPDE). These tools are designed to provide the research community with robust, reusable assets for scientific discovery. Advancing Responsible Open-Source AI through Cybersecurity and Biosafety Safeguards Tencent Hy is committed to advancing responsible open-source AI, incorporating safeguards throughout model training and release, with a strong emphasis on cybersecurity and biosafety to support the safe and responsible use of AI. Cybersecurity: Hy4 is trained on defensive security data, prioritizing proof-of-concept (PoC) development and vulnerability remediation. The model incorporates reverse engineering and penetration testing for analysis purposes. However, offensive materials related to exploitation are explicitly excluded from the training dataset. Cybersecurity experts from Tencent’s Xuanwu Lab and Keen Security Lab conducted security assessments covering cryptographic reverse engineering, binary deobfuscation, vulnerability exploitation, and more. The assessments found no significant concerns regarding Hy4’s offensive cybersecurity capabilities in the areas evaluated. Biosafety : Based on internal expert reviews, Hy4 demonstrates strong foundational biological knowledge; however, its capabilities in open-ended experimental design are more limited compared to frontier models. Delivering Greater Cost Performance, Hy4 Flash Recently Released Hy4 is currently available across Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom’s AI Assistant (Dayuan), ima, and more. Additionally, the model’s API is being made available via third-party platforms such as OpenRouter, Hermes, and OpenCode. Integration efforts are underway for other Tencent products and platforms, including QQ, Honor of Kings, Game of Peace, WeRead, and Tencent News. Guided by a core commitment to practical AI, Hy4 continues to push the boundaries of AI performance while delivering exceptional cost-effectiveness.

title: Hungary: Communist-era files released, up to 60k former agents revealed
abstract:
By Rita Konya & MTI Published on 4 November 2026 - 21:43 GMT+1 • Updated 5 November 2026 - 8:40 GMT+1 Hungary released communist-era secret police files Wednesday, identifying up to 60,000 informants, a path for Hungary in reckoning with its repressive past. In spite of Hungary's democratic transition in 1990, efforts to disclose communist-era archives have repeatedly failed, with critics blaming successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures across the political spectrum. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar ended this stall with a bill in September to grant unrestricted access for the public to the records for the first time. "After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives. "For decades, restrictions on public access provided opportunities for political hysteria, blackmail, the exertion of pressure, and silencing," he said. Public figures featured in registry Politicians, clergy members and TV personalities' names appeared in the registries. But a "large proportion" of the informants were "people who did not make their mark on national public life," said Bendeguz Gergo Cseh, the head of the archive. The government will set up hotlines offering emotional support and counselling for those affected by the revelations. "Following today's disclosure, a great many families will be confronted with information that is difficult for them to bear," Magyar said, asking people to treat the disclosure with "dignity and humanity." Various types of documents disclosed Under the law on the full disclosure of the previous regime’s secret service activities, four types of state security records dating from before 1990 will be made freely accessible to anyone. On Wednesday morning, the three of these became accessible on the nyitottaktak.hu (source in Hungarian) website. The "6 card" is the registration sheet for a network member. It contains the agent’s identifying data, including name, place and date of birth, mother’s name and occupation, but also the main details of the agent’s activity. Among them, the circumstances and motivations that led to them becoming an agent and how long they remained a network member. A register of recruitment between 1957 and 1962 and a database of former agents' personal data and code names were also released. In total, estimates suggest 50,000 to 60,000 agent names were made public over all this document disclosure. The public has free access since Wednesday to this data via a search tool that can filter by birth data, by name, place and date of birth, as well as by code name, across all types of records that have been made public. A second batch of files with further detail on about 9,000 informants will be released in February. Around 150,000 agents during communist era Hungary was under one-party communist rule between 1949 and 1989 that repressed dissent. Much like in East Germany and other parts of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, authorities employed an extensive network of informants to monitor public sentiment. Individuals, often recruited through coercion, were tasked with reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives for signs of disloyalty towards the regime. Estimates suggest that secret police employed around 150,000 agents in total over the four decades of the Mátyás Rákosi (1952-1953) and János Kádár (1956-1988) regimes. But only about one-third of their names are known, and detailed, substantive information exists for only about 10% of them. Many records were lost in 1956 and during the anti-Soviet change of regime, and the remainder was kept until 1997 in the Ministry of Interior, until the creation of ÁBTL’s predecessor, the Historical Office. Entrance of the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security in Budapest’s 6th district in Eötvös Street - 28 December 2022. MTI/Róka László Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, director general of the Historical Archives of State Security Services (ÁBTL), told the Hungarian press agency MTI that there are about ten thousand files, comprising many hundreds of thousands of pages in total. Responding to a question on how reliable and complete the documents are, Cseh Gergő Bendegúz underlined that the content of state security records is not necessarily true in every case and is certainly very incomplete. 'Better late than never' Debates over opening the archives have dogged Hungarian politics since the fall of communism. In 2002, weeks after becoming prime minister, socialist politician Peter Medgyessy became embroiled in a scandal after it was revealed that he had worked as a communist-era secret agent. The case prompted fresh calls for transparency, and parliament adopted a law in 2003 that allowed individuals who had been monitored to learn who had reported on them. The release was "better late than never," said historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation. "We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said. But historians have cautioned against judging anyone just because their names are on the list of informants. "I know of quite a few examples when someone was recruited, but they did not make a report, but in fact took a huge risk by turning against the authorities. Some even could be considered proper heroes," Eorsi stressed. title: EARL: The 3rd Workshop on Evaluating and Applying Recommender Systems with Large Language Models
abstract: This proposal outlines the organization of the 3rd Workshop on Evaluating and Applying Recommender Systems with Large Language Models (EARL), to be co-located with the 35th International ACM Conference on Knowledge and Information Management (CIKM 2026) in Rome, Italy. Following the strong engagement of the first two EARL editions, this third installment aims to solidify the workshop as a premier venue for advancing research at the intersection of large language models (LLMs) and recommender systems (RSs). EARL 2026 will foster discussions on the evaluation and practical deployment of LLM-driven RSs, emphasizing not only methodological soundness and reproducibility, but also the responsible integration of LLMs into real-world systems. By bringing together researchers and practitioners from academia and industry, the workshop will stimulate debate, encourage critical reflection, and shape future research directions in LLM-enhanced RSs.

title: Knowing When to Correct: Cost-Aware LLM Routing for OCR Post-Correction in Historical Documents
abstract: Historical digital archives present new challenges for retrieval systems because of OCR errors introduced by degraded page quality, old typefaces, and complex page layouts. Large language models (LLMs) offer an effective means of correcting transcription errors. However, applying LLM-based correction at scale can become prohibitively expensive. We investigate a selective, cost-aware strategy for LLM-assisted OCR post-correction, using a regression-guided router to predict when LLM correction is likely to improve transcription quality, thereby reducing unnecessary LLM processing and associated costs while preserving historically valid text. We evaluate this strategy on a dataset comprising historical Swiss newspapers published between 1733 and 1945. Our results show that selective correction can retain most of the quality gains of full correction while substantially reducing the LLM token cost. Using Tesseract OCR, sending all text segments for LLM correction improves CER from 6.3% to 2.9% (best approach). In contrast, our regression-guided router achieves CER of 3.1% (0.2% worse) while avoiding routing 40% of segments for LLM correction. Finally, we show that our regression-guided LLM router closely trails the decisions of an oracle that knows in advance which segments benefit from correction.

title: OneMall: One Architecture, More Scenarios — End-to-End Generative Recommender Family for E-commerce
abstract: In the wave of generative recommendation, we present OneMall, an end-to-end generative recommendation framework tailored for e-commerce services at Kuaishou. Our OneMall systematically unifies the e-commerce's multiple item distribution scenarios, such as Product-card, short-video and live-streaming. Specifically, it comprises three key components, aligning the entire model training pipeline to the LLM's pre-training/post-training: (1)E-commerce Semantic Tokenizer : we provide a tokenizer solution that captures both real-world semantics and business-specific item relations across different scenarios; (2)Transformer-based Architecture : we largely utilize Transformer as our model backbone, e.g., employing Query-Former for long sequence compression, Cross-Attention for multi-behavior sequence fusion, and Sparse MoE for scalable auto-regressive generation; (3)Reinforcement Learning Pipeline: we further connect retrieval and ranking models via RL, enabling the ranking model to serve as a reward signal for end-to-end policy retrieval model optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneMall achieves consistent improvements across all e-commerce scenarios: +14.7% GMV in Product-Card, +10.3% GMV in Short-Video, and +4.9% GMV in Live-Streaming. OneMall has been deployed, serving over 400 million daily active users at Kuaishou.

title: Follow the COMPASS: Reasoning-Guided Advertiser Bid Modeling for Campaign Simulation under Auction Dynamics
abstract: Advertisers launch ad campaigns to bid for potential customers and promote sales. In uncertain auction environments, accurate campaign performance forecasting (CPF) can help advertisers navigate toward efficient campaign configurations and successful marketing, much like a compass. However, existing CPF methods largely neglect auction dynamics, where competitors adjust their bids in response to evolving campaign states. Conventional log-driven models, which directly fit observable states to bid actions, overlook the deliberate reasoning process underlying advertiser behavior, leading to suboptimal forecasts. To fill the gap, we propose COMPASS, a reasoning-driven framework for modeling bid behavior during ad campaigns. COMPASS explicitly treats bid reasoning as a latent variable and progressively infers it under a Search-Optimization framework. Instead of a naive brute-force search, COMPASS adopts a hierarchical inference strategy: a high-capacity schema model searches over compact, high-level bid strategies, while a lightweight execution model expands them into concrete bid predictions and provides evaluation feedback. To simplify online deployment, we further propose an alignment-as-distillation mechanism with a self-evaluation trick. This avoids a separate knowledge distillation stage and produces a self-contained execution model that can be independently deployed without invoking the schema model at serving time. Extensive experiments on industrial and public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of COMPASS. In large-scale online A/B tests, COMPASS achieves a 5.1% uplift in average revenue per user, validating its practical impact in real-world advertising systems.

title: Do Large Language Models have Lateral Thinking in Puzzle-Solving Games?
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show exceptional skills in a wide range of tasks, with their ability in lateral thinking standing out as a particularly intriguing area. Lateral thinking in LLMs allows them to understand deeper or suggested meanings from the context, which is essential for making sense of complex scenarios, especially in puzzle-solving games. To delve deeper into and improve the lateral thinking capabilities of LLMs in the realm of puzzle-solving, we introduce the ''Lateral Thinking Puzzles'' and construct the accompanying dataset. Our novel Puzzle Verse framework aims to enhance LLMs' lateral thinking in puzzle-solving games. Complementing this, we propose a creativity metric to ensure comprehensive evaluations. Experiments show that the selected LLMs, after being trained with Puzzle Verse, have an average improvement of 93.1% compared to their performance before Puzzle Verse training among all metrics. We also validate the robustness of Puzzle Verse that trained LLMs perform better in other reasoning tasks.

title: PRISM: Pruning-Enhanced Intent Sampling for Recommendation Multi-List Generation
abstract: Generative recommendation has emerged as a prominent paradigm, unifying retrieval and ranking through large-scale sequence transducers. However, existing generative recommenders are basically pointwise: they optimize for next-item prediction, leaving the construction of the final exposure list---a slate---to heuristic post-processing. This creates a structural gap between pointwise candidate generation and industrial listwise delivery, which demands holistic reasoning over contextual opportunity, position bias, and intent uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce List Composer, a decoupled module that transforms pointwise candidate pools into deliverable exposure lists within generative recommender systems. We instantiate this concept through PRISM, an autoregressive listwise generation model featuring two core mechanisms. First, a CVAE-based IntentSampler module models user interests as a latent distribution, sampling distinct intent facets as initial states averts the Deterministic Collapse phenomenon, wherein standard autoregressive generators converge onto nearly identical sequences despite repeated decoding. Second, a Listwise Pruning strategy dynamically culls low-utility beam paths using position-discounted pointwise scores, concentrating computational resources on promising trajectories. Extensive offline experiments and real-world online A/B tests validate the effectiveness of PRISM, which achieves consistent improvements in recommendation quality and serving efficiency, including a 0.288% gain in video views on a major short-video platform.

title: RankGap-RAG: Rank-Discrepancy Contrastive Feedback for Multi-Paraphrase Retrieval
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is sensitive to the wording of the original query, and iterative query refinement can further amplify early retrieval errors when misleading passages are reused as feedback. We propose RankGap-RAG, a training-free query refinement framework that uses bi-encoder/cross-encoder rank discrepancy to select inference-time hard-negative feedback. Rather than treating retrieved passages as uniformly useful feedback, RankGap-RAG pairs cross-encoder-selected positive evidence with rank-gap negatives to guide the LLM toward relevant evidence while discouraging misleading semantic directions. We further introduce a Diverse Multi-Chain extension that combines contrastive feedback with multiple refinement trajectories. Experiments on SQuAD 2.0, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue show consistent gains over original-query retrieval, while component ablations on SQuAD 2.0 and Natural Questions show improvements over positive-only feedback.

title: Ed-Alpha: An Open Benchmark for Predicting Investment-Relevant Corporate Events from Open Data
abstract: We present Ed-Alpha, an open benchmark platform for predicting and evaluating investment-relevant corporate events using public data. Existing event-driven investment research often relies on expensive, proprietary data, making methods difficult to reproduce or compare. Ed-Alpha addresses this challenge by providing a transparent and fully reproducible pipeline. Specifically, it uses regulatory filings from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as ground-truth event labels and combines them with high-volume news signals from the GDELT project. Using Ed-Alpha, our initial analysis reveals that even state-of-the-art LLMs achieve only limited effectiveness in predicting corporate events; we therefore expect the platform to facilitate more efficient and transparent experimentation toward future improvements in effectiveness. The benchmark platform and a demonstration video, as well as all related code and methods, are available in our repository. https://github.com/E9Technologies/ed-alpha

title: S-VEAM: A Shared Spectral Memory for Cross-Session Retrieval in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents in multi-session deployments must answer through a bounded prompt window while their histories grow without bound. Surfacing the right history within that budget is a retrieval and ranking problem over a state that never stops growing. We present S-VEAM, a shared spectral memory controller for long-session agents in which construction and retrieval are two phases of one persistent spectral state (P, V, ?) that unifies writing new sessions into the state and reading evidence back out. Both phases use non-generative spectral operations: the controller issues no generative-LLM call at memory-management time, and the spectral indexing rank — distinct from the retained verbatim pool — remains fixed as trajectories grow. In the tested long-session settings this yields a low-latency retrieval profile while preserving verbatim evidence for the downstream model. We evaluate S-VEAM under the Cross-Session Stress Test Protocol (CSSTP), a source-faithful evaluation over existing benchmarks with controlled long-session stress conditions. LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S provide the main long-session evidence: S-VEAM is top-ranked on both answer containment and evidence-backed answer containment on every LoCoMo cell and on LongMemEval-S native, with non-generative fixed-rank maintenance and low-latency retrieval. MuSiQue Tier 3 enters as an auxiliary multi-hop evidence-split diagnostic where S-VEAM achieves the highest evidence-backed answer containment. Stateful memory peers enter as cost-matched counterparts under the same budget and reset policy. S-VEAM thus marks a fixed-rank, non-generative indexing operating point for long-session memory under tight retrieval budgets.

title: A Hybrid Framework for Time Series Anomaly Detection with LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for time series anomaly detection (TSAD), yet their direct use often remains inferior to methods designed specifically for TSAD. In this work, we study whether this limitation arises primarily from weak forecasting or from insufficient exploitation of forecast residuals. Across LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, we find that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can improve forecasting accuracy, but does not consistently improve anomaly detection under fixed residual thresholding. The primary driver of detection performance is not forecasting quality, but how the resulting residuals are analyzed and refined in subsequent stages. Motivated by this finding, we propose a Forecaster–Detector–Imputer pipeline that restricts the LLM to forecasting normal temporal behavior, applies classical detectors to the resulting residuals using adaptive windowing and contamination-aware thresholding, and refines candidate detections through imputation via a time-series foundation model followed by a second detection pass. The proposed framework reaches F1 = 0.789 with LLaMA and F1 = 0.785 with Mistral, roughly doubling the zero-shot baselines, with results confirmed on an independent NAB benchmark. These results suggest that LLMs are most effective for TSAD when used as forecasting components within a hybrid residual-analysis pipeline, and that the primary bottleneck lies in post-hoc residual exploitation rather than forecasting quality alone.

title: OPERA: Option-level Pedagogical Explanation via Reasoning for Augmented Knowledge Tracing
abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) aims to predict learners' future performance by modeling their historical interaction data. In real-world educational scenarios, multiple-choice questions are deliberately designed so that each distractor exposes a specific misconception; however, existing KT models rely on randomly initialized ID embeddings and reduce each interaction to a binary correctness label, making it difficult to exploit such option-level diagnostic signals. To address these problems, we propose an option-level pedagogical explanation framework for augmented KT, i.e., OPERA, which combines LLM-based option-level explanation generation, multi-judge quality assurance, and offline semantic embedding injection into existing KT backbones, with all LLM computation confined to one-time offline preprocessing. Experiments on three multiple-choice datasets demonstrate our framework's superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy, consistently improving lightweight ID-based backbones to match or surpass much heavier process-aware models. To encourage reproducible research, we have made our code publicly available at https://pykt.org/.

title: Modeling Uncertainty in LLM-Based Information Retrieval Evaluation via Hierarchical Bayesian Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in Information Retrieval (IR) evaluation to annotate query-document pairs for relevance, enabling significant cost reductions compared to the traditional human-only assessment process. However, LLM-generated human judgements are not error-free and, compared to humans, are more prone to introducing systematic latent biases and producing spurious results. Therefore, since the evaluation target remains the human, it is necessary to understand how to align observations derived from LLM-generated annotations with those that would have been made using human relevance judgments. This work introduces a novel framework for estimating the performance we would observe if relevance judgements were human-made, using a large amount of LLM-generated judgments with a limited pool of human-annotated queries. The proposed approach exploits hierarchical Bayesian modeling and calibration to build Credible Intervals (CrIs) providing statistical guarantees on the estimated performance. The obtained results show how the computed CrIs allow (a) over 95% coverage while exploiting a limited number of human annotations and (b) to jointly take into account the LLM error and the variance due to topics, enabling future use of the computed CrIs for statistical hypothesis testing.

title: Query Explorer: Domain-Aware Hierarchical Query Suggestions for Exploratory Search
abstract: Large content catalogs present a fundamental discovery challenge: users often lack the vocabulary or domain knowledge to formulate queries that surface the most relevant content. Existing suggestion systems, built on co-occurrence data, only reflect historical search behavior, leaving vast portions of the catalog undiscovered. This paper presents Query Explorer, which uses a frontier LLM to generate domain-aware hierarchical concept trees for exploratory search, helping users both narrow broad queries into specific subcategories and discover related concepts they may not have considered. Concept trees are generated offline and surfaced as interactive suggestion pills, guiding users from broad intent toward concrete queries (e.g., food → potluck invitation → Thanksgiving potluck flyer). We instantiate and evaluate Query Explorer on Adobe Express, a creative template marketplace, with trees generated across five levels of specificity for 1,000 head queries scoped for an A/B test. Over 18 days, template click-through rate increased by 0.5 percentage points (99.4% confidence), while template export rate — our primary business metric — declined by 1.1 percentage points (97.6% confidence). User feedback points to the multi-level pill navigation, not the underlying suggestions, as the likely driver of this tension, a distinction with direct implications for how LLM-generated discovery interfaces should be designed. The architecture itself is domain-agnostic, adaptable to any catalog by changing only the prompt's domain constraints.

title: CaLR: Context-Aware Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Sequential recommendation aims to model users' evolving preferences from their historical interactions. Recent latent reasoning methods improve sequential recommenders by extending inferencetime computation in continuous representation space, refining user representations without generating explicit reasoning text. However, existing methods mainly reason over the encoded history itself and make limited use of contextual feedback from users' recent interactions. Such feedback, especially positive and negative signals in the latest session, can not only complement the long-term user representation but also provide directional guidance for latent reasoning by indicating which preference patterns should be strengthened or suppressed. In this paper, we propose Context-Aware Latent Reasoning (CaLR), a model-agnostic framework that grounds latent reasoning in session-level context. From the input perspective, CaLR selects informative positive and negative items from users' recent sessions as reasoning anchors. From the architecture perspective, it injects these anchors into each reasoning step through a Cross-Attention-based module. From the optimization perspective, it introduces Process Supervision Loss (PSL) to supervise intermediate reasoning states according to anchor feedback polarity. Experiments on two real-world public benchmarks show that CaLR consistently improves multiple sequential recommendation backbones and outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and further analyses verify the effectiveness of each component in CaLR. Moreover, a seven-day online A/B test on Kuaishou Lite demonstrates its effectiveness in real-world industrial deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/Ak4ne-windsky/CaLR.

title: Less Is More: Knowledge Graph Construction and Schema-Guided Canonicalization with LLMs
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are widely used in domains such as healthcare and finance, but existing LLM-based construction methods often produce redundant triples and semantically inconsistent representations. We propose a unified framework combining LLM-based triple extraction with schema-guided canonicalization. Our approach extracts triples and induces a schema to constrain canonicalization candidates, enabling consistent entity and relation merging. Experiments on five benchmark datasets show that our method produces more compact KGs with higher F1 scores than existing approaches. Ablation studies show that schema-guided canonicalization reduces redundancy with minimal loss of semantic fidelity. Our canonicalized KGs also improve retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) question-answering performance. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HwangSeonPark/less-is-more-kg

title: SKG-KT: Semantic Knowledge Graph Construction and Reasoning for Knowledge Tracing by Large Language Models
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT), a core component of intelligent tutoring systems, aims to model the dynamic evolution of students' knowledge states based on their historical interaction data. However, mainstream methods rely heavily on large-scale students' response logs, hindering generalization to unseen students, and often overlook the semantic structure of knowledge points in knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we propose Semantic Knowledge Graph-Based Knowledge Tracing (SKG-KT), a novel KT framework that leverages the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) to enhance the modelling of unseen students, without relying on numerous students with historical records. SKG-KT consists of two stages: ATC-ruled Semantic Graph Extraction and a Concept-aware Reasoning mechanism. In the first stage, we design a semantic student knowledge graph extraction method grounded in ATC rules, which captures the semantic structure across three hierarchical layers—domain, cluster, and standard—aligned with established educational theory. To extend beyond mathematics, we further introduce a multi-disciplinary semantic graph extraction method that induces an ATC-inspired hierarchical schema for other disciplines via LLM-based label induction. In the second stage, the Concept-aware Reasoning mechanism first applies knowledge concept reasoning to infer key knowledge concepts for unseen students with limited previous student data, and then fine-tunes an open-source LLM for correctness prediction based on the reasoned knowledge concepts, adapting the LLM to the KT task. Extensive experiments conducted on three publicly available educational benchmark datasets, namely Xes3g5m-small, Xes3g5m-large, and MOOCRadar, demonstrate that SKG-KT achieves state-of-the-art performance in knowledge tracing. Furthermore, SKG-KT has been validated to achieve robust predictive performance compared to others, while relying on a limited number of students with historical records. Our code and prompts are publicly available at the link . https://github.com/linqingliDestinyController/SKG_KT/tree/main.

title: 1ShotBench: Demonstrating One-Shot Prompt Reproducibility for Autonomous Coding Agents
abstract: The growing use of LLM agents raises a reproducibility problem: given the same task specification, different agents may follow different workflows, consume different resources, and produce varying artifacts and outcomes. We introduce the concept of One-Shot Prompt Reproducibility (1SPR): the consistency of one-shot execution across different agents given a fixed specification, without iterative human guidance. To operationalize this, we present 1ShotBench, a toolkit that repeatedly executes the same product requirement document (PRD) across isolated agent workspaces, capturing full traces, artifacts, and metadata, along with an LLM judge to evaluate results. We demonstrate a case study using software engineering tasks built around the Anserini information retrieval toolkit, though our system itself supports arbitrary tasks. 1ShotBench allows users to compare runs side by side, inspect how execution and implementation paths diverge despite a shared specification, and analyze how workflow differences relate to cost, latency, and correctness. Our central contribution is a reproducibility-oriented lens for examining agentic software development.

title: LCSR-LLM: Longitudinal Cognitive State Reasoning for LLM-based Knowledge Tracing
abstract: Knowledge tracing aims to infer a student's evolving mastery from historical learning interactions. Recent large language model (LLM) approaches offer a natural way to encode textualized learning histories, but they are often evaluated primarily as next-step predictors. This leaves open whether the model forms a stable and diagnostically meaningful latent trajectory of student state, or merely exploits shallow statistics such as recent correctness rates. We introduce LCSR-LLM, a longitudinal cognitive state reasoning framework that uses marker-aligned LLM hidden states to estimate a soft latent cognitive-state trajectory at each prediction step. The framework combines state-conditioned prediction with trajectory-level regularization, especially dynamic consistency and entropy control, to encourage smoother and non-collapsed state posteriors. We further propose Longitudinal Aggregation Drift (LAD), a diagnostic protocol that measures sequence-level prediction drift, posterior uncertainty, and trajectory volatility. On ASSIST2012, LCSR-LLM with Qwen2.5-7B reaches 0.7684 AUC, 0.7705 ACC, and 0.8610 F1, achieving the best AUC among our controlled runs and the best F1 among the listed results, while remaining competitive in ACC. Paired trajectory diagnostics show that dynamic consistency and entropy control improve internal trajectory behavior beyond final predictive accuracy.

title: Preserving LLM Output Distributions for Probabilistic Query Evaluation
abstract: Language models can be used to augment databases; typically, when this is done, their top prediction is used while the uncertainty in this prediction is ignored. We propose a framework that preserves output distributions from language model predictions and uses them to evaluate SQL queries probabilistically. First, a language model is used to infer new features from existing ones. Second, ProvSQL, a PostgreSQL extension implementing a probabilistic database through data provenance, encodes the predictions as mutually exclusive events in a provenance circuit and evaluates probabilistic queries. We extend ProvSQL to support text-value comparisons and join operations on language model predictions. We demonstrate the framework on 10\,612 Amazon musical products and 230\,156 user reviews, locally augmented with the Llama 3.1 model. We show that probabilistic querying reveals contradictions between model predictions and existing labels, recovers data records otherwise missed, and propagates joint uncertainty across multi-table queries.

title: SAERec: Constructing Fine-grained Interpretable Intent Priors via Sparse Autoencoders for Recommendation
abstract: Intent-based recommender systems have gained significant attention for enhancing accuracy and interpretability by modeling the underlying motivations behind user behaviors. Most existing models derive intents directly from user sequences via clustering or prototype learning. However, they are sensitive to the sequence quality, require presetting the number of intents and lack explicit semantic grounding. These issues lead to an incomplete and coarse intent set and limit the effectiveness of recommendation. In this paper, we propose the Sparse Autoencoder for intent-based recommendation (SAERec), a novel recommender that automatically constructs a fine-grained, interpretable intent space from a textual corpus to guide recommendation. Rather than treating texts as side signals, SAERec leverages them as high-information-density evidence for intent construction. Specifically, we first extract a comprehensive set of fine-grained interpretable intents from the latent space of Large Language Models (LLMs) by using a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to disentangle and interpret text embeddings, which isolates intent-related semantics from substantial textual noise. Then, for each user, we retrieve relevant intents from the set as priors to guide recommendation. These priors include personal intents that match each user's current interests and public intents that capture general item patterns shared across users (e.g., ''quality'' and ''price''). Finally, to integrate retrieved intents into sequence modeling, we propose a multi-branch attention mechanism that captures temporal dependencies and injects both personal and public intent signals, followed by an adaptive fusion layer to construct the final user representation for recommendation. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of SAERec, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while providing human-understandable explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangnanx129/SAERec.

title: Beyond Rote Memorization: A Cognitive Framework for Tracing Knowledge in Open-World Scenarios
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) models commonly represent exercises with learned problem identifiers, which limits their ability to handle new problems whose IDs have not accumulated sufficient interactions. We propose MKT-LLM, a content-aware framework for new-problem KT that combines problem-content representations with learner interaction history in an LLM-compatible latent space. The framework contains three components: (1) Perceptual Harmonization, which fuses learned problem embeddings with semantic content embeddings; (2) Adaptive Generalization, which synthesizes an ID-like representation for an unseen problem from semantically similar seen problems; and (3) Cognitive Synthesis, which models the learner's evolving knowledge state from the resulting interaction sequence. MKT-LLM uses content similarity to place new problems in the same latent space as observed problems and performs prediction from latent states rather than relying on token-level answer generation. Experiments on NIPS2020 and Junyi show consistent improvements over representative KT and cold-start baselines, and the model degrades more gracefully as the proportion of new problems increases.

title: LLMJudge: Meta-Evaluating Automatic Relevance Judgments
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to produce the relevance labels that underpin the evaluation of information retrieval (IR) and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Yet delegating relevance assessment to an LLM raises a meta-evaluation question that is hard to answer with existing resources: when, and how much, can we trust an automatic judge? We present LLMJudge, a resource for meta-evaluating LLM-generated relevance judgments. LLMJudge collects 42 complete judgment sets over the TREC 2023 Deep Learning track, spanning fine-tuned, proprietary, and open-source models and a wide range of prompting strategies. Each judgment set is paired with official human qrels, enabling two complementary axes of analysis: label agreement with human assessors (e.g., Cohen's κ, Krippendorff's α) and system-ranking fidelity (e.g., Kendall's τ, Spearman's ρ). Beyond the data, we release a standardized format, baselines, and an evaluation harness so that new judges can be plugged in and compared reproducibly. Our analysis shows that high label agreement is neither necessary nor sufficient for faithful system ranking, that open-source judges are markedly more stable than proprietary ones, and that fine-tuning improves correlation at the cost of reliability. LLMJudge is publicly available and provides a reusable testbed for auditing the judges who increasingly judge our systems. Full resources, data, and detailed results are available at https://llm4eval.github.io/LLMJudge-benchmark/.

title: CDAR-RAG: Cross-Distributional Alignment-Based Retriever for Online Community Jargon Understanding
abstract: Online communities often use jargon, which is a set of specialized terms that can only be understood implicitly and in context by a specific group of users. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable achievements in various tasks, understanding community jargon is challenging, as it introduces more complex, high-context comprehension. In-context learning (ICL) can help LLMs achieve better jargon understanding by providing demonstrations of jargon usage-definition pairs, yet using appropriate demonstrations is critical. However, which jargon terms are appropriate demonstrations for the given target jargon term is unclear; no true relationship between jargon terms is known. This makes typical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) struggle to obtain appropriate demonstrations, as labeled query-document relations are often required for task-specialized RAG. For this problem, we propose CDAR (Cross-Distributional Alignment-based Retriever), a retriever training method that requires no explicit query-document relevance labels, by aligning the distribution of cosine similarities between pairs of jargon usage examples to that between their corresponding definitions. Our results show that CDAR effectively increases jargon understanding across five LLM generators of varying scales, consistently outperforming zero-shot, random, vanilla RAG, and triplet-loss baselines, and that a retriever trained on one jargon domain transfers effectively to unseen jargon domains. Notably, Qwen3 8B + CDAR significantly surpasses GPT-OSS 120B performance, showing that CDAR serves as an efficient framework, especially with smaller LLMs.

title: CiteAlign-Table: Verifying Citation Faithfulness when LLMs Attribute to Structured Data
abstract: Attributed Question Answering systems increasingly ground answers in tabular structured corpora—Wikipedia infoboxes and relational tables, the dominant structured evidence in open-domain RAG—yet citation faithfulness methods remain designed for text passages. This mismatch allows LLMs to cite the correct table but the wrong row, silently aggregate values without justification, or attribute claims to schema fields that do not semantically entail them. We formalize multiple structural hallucination modes specific to structured-data attribution and introduce CiteAlign-Table, a hybrid neuro-symbolic verifier that checks schema-path validity, cell-level semantic alignment, and arithmetic consistency between claims and their cited records. A schema-aware entailment module detects entity and content misalignments, while a lightweight program synthesizer verifies numerical aggregation, temporal consistency, and unit correctness. Experiments on a hybrid benchmark of Wikipedia infoboxes and WikiTables show that CiteAlign-Table achieves 0.84 F1 in detecting unfaithful structured citations, while text-only baselines degrade to 0.61 F1. By extending citation faithfulness from passages to structured records, our work makes attributed QA trustworthy over the heterogeneous data that production RAG systems actually retrieve.

title: FedICL-KVc: Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly constrained by the scarcity of high-quality public data, making private data essential for further improvement. However, private data is typically distributed across resource-constrained devices and cannot be shared due to strict privacy requirements, rendering conventional federated fine-tuning of LLMs impractical under limited computation and communication budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache (FedICL-KVc), a novel framework that enables effective utilization of private data without parameter updates. Instead of transmitting raw demonstrations, clients upload only the corresponding key--value (KV) caches generated during auto-regressive inference, which are compact, smaller than full-model parameter payloads, and subject to an empirical reconstruction-risk evaluation under a restricted attack model. To further enhance efficiency and effectiveness, we introduce a confidence-based demonstration selection strategy to identify informative client samples, and a server-side KV cache compression method guided by a proxy dataset to reduce inference cost and suppress irrelevant information. Experiments on multiple tasks demonstrate that FedICL-KVc achieves competitive performance without client-side parameter updates or full-model parameter transmission while avoiding direct raw-data transmission.
