title: ResCrime: Residual Evolution Diffusion for Spatially Adaptive Multimodal Urban Crime Forecasting
abstract: Urban crime forecasting aims to predict future spatial risk distributions from historical crime and urban context, supporting proactive public safety allocation. Existing methods have advanced this task with multimodal urban signals, but they often use historical crime risk maps only as conditioning inputs, without explicitly modeling their evolution into future risk maps. They also provide limited adaptation of point-of-interest (POI) semantics to local historical crime context, weakening their ability to capture spatially varying predictive relevance. To address these issues, we propose ResCrime, a history-anchored residual evolution diffusion framework for spatially adaptive multimodal crime forecasting. ResCrime initializes the reverse diffusion near the observed historical risk map and models future risk as a residual evolution of historical observations. A multimodal denoising backbone integrates crime, POI, satellite, and map features to support history-to-future risk estimation, while Crime History Spatial Adaptive Reweighting (CSAR) recalibrates POI semantic channels based on local historical intensity before multimodal fusion. Experiments on New York City and Los Angeles demonstrate that ResCrime outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving AP over DiffCrime by 6.68% and 5.21% and reducing RMSE by 10.71% and 6.52%, while maintaining efficient inference. Code is available at https://github.com/RooB1t/ResCrime.

title: Asymmetric Privileged Distillation for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and vision--language models have introduced richer semantic guidance into Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection (WS-VAD). However, video-dependent text generation or encoding during inference introduces substantial computational overhead and complicates deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. We propose APD-VAD, an Asymmetric Privileged Distillation framework that uses LVLM-generated descriptions as privileged information during training and deploys a visual student without dynamic text processing. A Privileged Language Cascade (PLC) supplies video- and snippet-level descriptions to the teacher, and a Background-Debiased Graph (BDG) attenuates scene-dominated relations before temporal graph reasoning. Semantic-distribution, feature, and topology distillation transfer the resulting class, snippet, and relational knowledge to the student. At inference, a dual-branch visual graph and Visual Prototype Memory (VPM) provide category-aware visual context through cached category prototypes and class-routed visual retrieval. Experiments on UCF-Crime and XD-Violence demonstrate competitive anomaly detection and improved fine-grained temporal localization, while deployment profiling confirms efficient inference without recurring LVLM processing. Code is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/APD-VAD.

title: Interpretation-Aware Image Manipulation Detection
abstract: Image manipulation has been a common practice since the early days of photography, and has evolved into a sophisticated threat with the rise of powerful image editing tools and generative AI. It can be used to spread misinformation, manipulate public opinion, and cause harm to individuals and communities. In this article, we study the problem of determining whether an image is misleading, i.e. edited in a misleading way. We introduce a risk framework to assess the intrinsic interpretive shift (ITS) of an ordered image pair, which evaluates whether the final edited image changes the interpretation supported by a source reference image. We show our risk framework can be operationalized with the Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) provenance framework. We estimate ITS with a single-call vision-language implementation of our risk framework, which first checks for meaningful visual differences, then tests whether the differences induce interpretive shift, and finally determines whether the shift is fully explained by permissible transformations rather than content-level changes. The system outputs a binary label (potentially misleading or not) together with interpretive clues and a short justification. To test the approach and show that ITS is a measurable proxy for misleading edits, we built a benchmark of 418 ordered pairs, drawn from real-world fact-check cases and meaning-preserving transformations. The best-performing model configuration (gpt-5.4) achieves 88.2% precision, 94.2% recall, and 96.5% balanced accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/liyu0x/ITS_detection/.
